----------------------------------------

Instructor: Welcome to the Spring Security Zero to Master course. For majority of us, security is a complex and boring topic. But if you master the Spring Security framework and try to implement security with the help of this framework, then it is going to be super fun and interesting. Spring Security is a de-facto standard framework for implementing security inside any Spring-based applications. If you're a Java developer, regardless of what kind of application you are trying to build with the help of Spring ecosystem, it can be an monolithic application or it can be an MVC application or it can be an simple backend application with the REST APIs or it can be an microservices application or it can be an full-stack application where on the front-end you have Angular or React, and on the backend you have a Spring Boot application.

So regardless of what kind of application you are trying to build as a Java developer, you can happily use Spring Security framework to implement and enforce security inside your application. This course, it is going to help you to master this Spring Security framework. I know you may have too many questions around the agenda of this course, what I'm going to cover inside this course, so let's try to quickly understand what I'm going to cover inside this course.

At the starting of the course, I'll take you into the world of Spring Security. I'll give the introduction about this framework, followed by we are going to start securing a web application using the Spring Security framework. Once we start securing a web application using this framework, in the same process, we are also going to explore all the important interfaces, classes, annotations that belongs to the Spring Security framework. So this knowledge is going to help in clearing any kind of interviews around the Spring Security framework.

I'm also going to teach you how to configure authentication and authorization rules inside a web application. Once we are clear with all these basic concepts, we will move on to the advanced concepts like how to implement role-based access mechanism using roles and authorities inside an application. What are the different strategies that Spring Security is going to provide when we are dealing with the passwords? Passwords are not supposed to store with the plain text value.

We need to follow certain standards like hashing. So I'm going to teach you everything around the security standards as well, like hashing when coming to the passwords. Followed by I'm also going to teach you on how to secure your Java methods by using the method-level security of Spring Security framework. Spring Security framework also make developers life easy in handling various security attacks like CSRF, CORS. Followed by towards the end of the course, we are going to talk in detail about JWT tokens. LECTURE 1.8: Quick introduction to Servlets & Filters
----------------------------------------

Presenter: One of the toughest questions that you can expect around the Spring security framework inside interviews is around the Spring security internal flow. The interviewer can ask you a simple question, which is, "Can you please explain me what is the internal architecture or internal flow of Spring security framework?" Throughout this course, we're going to put lot of efforts to understand how Spring security works internally, and you can see in this slide I have a high level Spring security internal flow.

I'm going to teach you this internal flow inside the next lecture in a detailed manner. But before we try to understand the Spring security internal flow, first you need to understand what are servlets and filters inside Java ecosystem. There is a strong reason why I am trying to explain about servlets and filters, because inside the Spring security framework, also, lot of security related functionality is implemented with the help of filters and servlets.

I hope you're convinced on why we're discussing these servlets and filters. First, let's try to understand what is a servlet, later on we can try to understand what is a filter. We all know the backend code that we write with the programming language like Java, it is going to be deployed into your server. Anyone who want to invoke the rest API or the MVC path that is hosted inside my server, they can easily invoke with the help of the browser, which is one of the client application.

Whenever someone is trying to send a request with the help of browser, the request, it is going to come in a HTTP or HTTPS protocol. So whatever message we are trying to send with this HTTP protocol, it is not going to make any sense to the backend server or backend logic that we have returned. Inside Java programming language, anything that we want to process, it has to be converted into your Java object. So this is where the servlet container comes into picture.

So what is a servlet container? It is a kind of web server or app server, We have many servlet containers like Tomcat, JBoss, so these are all the examples of servlet containers or app servers or web servers. So you can see, all my code is deployed inside a web or app server. So what is the responsibility of these apps server or web server? It is going to convert whatever HTTP request that we are going to receive into an ServletRequest object or HTTP ServletRequest object.

Inside the ServletRequest or inside these HTTP ServletRequest object, the data that is sent by client application is going to be present. So once the servlet request object is prepared, the same is going to be forwarded to the corresponding servlet like you can see here. So these servlets is going to be leveraged by the frameworks like Spring boot or Spring security. From these servlets, only the actual business logic invocation is going to happen.

Like whatever business logic we write inside the controller classes or inside the service classes, all that business logic is going to be invoked from these servlets only. As of now we discuss the story of the request, but once the request is processed on the backend server, the backend server or the backend code, it is going to respond to the client with the response. So the response is going to be sent in the form of ServletResponse object. Again, this ServletResponse object, it is not going to make any sense to the client application or to the browser.

Here, also the Servlet Container come into picture, the servlet container, before it is trying to forward the response to the client application, it is going to convert the ServletResponse object into the HTTP or HTTPS protocol, before Spring boot framework or before Spring framework introduce somewhere in early 2000s, every developer they used to write all their business logic with the help of servlets only. Building a business logic or building a web application with the servlets is very complex, frameworks like Spring boot or Spring security, they are going to do a lot of heavy lifting for the developers.

These days we are enjoying the benefits of these frameworks. We as a developers, we are just trying to make some configurations and once we do some minimum configurations, we are more focused on writing the business logic. We are nowhere worrying about how to build a servlet, how to build a filter, because everything is being taken care by the frameworks these days. I hope you're clear of the servlet, now let's try to understand what is a filter and what is the role of it?

You can see in the picture, before my request reaching to the actual servlet, there are filters in between. With this, it should be pretty clear for you, filters inside Java web applications, they're going to be used to intercept each and every request and response that is traveling between client and actual servlets or actual business logic. Using these filters only frameworks like Spring security, they are implementing lot of security related logic.

For example, what is the purpose of Spring security framework? The purpose of the Spring security framework is very simple. Whenever we are trying to access a REST API or a MVC path, it has to intercept the request and it has to identify if the user is authenticated or not, if not, it has to redirect the user to the login page. Since the Spring security has to intercept each and every request to enforce the security inside a web application, all the security logic of Spring security framework is implemented with the help of filters, only.

When we start exploring internal architecture of Spring security, you'll be able see there are not many filters playing a role inside the Spring security framework. Using these filters only the framework is going to do lot of magic of enforcing the security. I hope you are clear with all these discussion around the servlets and filters, please note that always the filters, they are going to be executed first, followed by the servlets or the actual business logic is going to be executed.

So this is a simple definition that you can remember for now. From the next lecture, let's try to explore the internal architecture of Spring security framework. Thank you, bye!

LECTURE 1.9: Introduction to Spring Security Internal flow - Theory
----------------------------------------

Instructor: Before I try to explain you about the Spring Security internal flow, I want to share a disclaimer. There is a very good chance that you may not understand anything from this lecture because we need to deep dive into the Spring Security Framework to understand all these internal components. But I'll try my best to make this lecture as clear as possible, but don't get demotivated if you're not able to remember anything from this lecture.

That's perfectly fine. Throughout this course, we are going to revisit the same internal flow many times and we're also going to discuss each component in detail. By the end of this course, you're going to remember this internal flow forever. I hope you're clear with this disclaimer. Now, let's try to understand the internal flow of Spring Security Framework. In the very first step, some client application, like a browser or it can be a mobile application or it can be a postman, through these client applications, the end users, they're going to send a request to access REST API or a MVC path.

If they're trying to access a protected API, obviously, the end user, they have to provide their credentials as part of the RequestHeader or RequestBody based upon the configurations that we have done behind the scenes. If the user is trying to access a protected API without mentioning credentials, we know what is going to happen. The Spring Security Framework, it is going to redirect the user to the login page to enter his or her credentials. So this job of identifying if the user is authenticated or not is going to be done by the Spring Security filters.

Like I was telling in the previous lecture, filters, they're going to play an important role in intercepting each and every request. Inside the Spring Security Framework also, there are more than 20 different filters intercepting each and every request and handling the scenario specific to them. For example, there is a filter inside the Spring Security Framework to identify if the user is authenticated or not. If the user is not authenticated, the responsibility of that filter is to redirect to the login page.

And similarly, there is a filter to detect the CSRF attack. So there are good amount of filters which we're going to explore throughout this course. But the point that you need to understand here is, as soon as a client send a request to the backend API, which is being secured by a Spring Security Framework, the request is going to be intercepted by the Spring Security filters. Based upon your configurations, 5 or 10 or 15 or 20 filters, they're going to process your request one by one.

At any layer, if there is an error, then the end user will get an 401 error or 403 error based upon the exception type. Think like the end user provided the proper credentials inside the request when he's trying to access a secured API. In such scenarios, what is going to happen is the Spring Security filters, they're going to populate the authentication object inside the step two. We know by default, the credentials that we receive from the end user, they are going to be in the HTTP request object since we can't forward the same HTTP servlet request object throughout the framework code and throughout the business logic.

The very first responsibility of the Spring Security filters is going to be to convert the credentials from the HTTP servlet request object to authentication object. Inside this authentication object, there'll be fields like username, password and there is also a boolean to identify whether the user is authenticated or not. So initially when these object is created very first time, this isAuthenticated boolean value is going to be set as false. Apart from that, the username and password, they're also going to be populated like easybytes is a username in our case and password is going to be 12345.

The same authentication object is going to be used by all other components inside the Spring Security Framework. So you can assume this authentication object is a common contract which can be understand by all the components inside the Spring Security Framework. And these authentication object represents an user credentials and it also has an information to identify if the user is authenticated or not. So once the authentication object is populated, the filters that are going to forward the request to the authentication manager.

So who is this fellow authentication manager? This authentication manager is going to take the responsibility of completing the authentication and conveying the results back to the filters whether the authentication is successful or not. So this authentication manager will say, "Hey filters, don't worry. You give me the authentication object with the username, password, I'm going to take the responsibility of authenticating the user by taking help from other components.

Once all authentication logic is executed, I'm going to convey you the results." So that's assurance the authentication manager is going to give to the Spring Security filters. Please note that these authentication manager, it is only going to take the responsibility of completing the authentication, but it is not going to do the actual authentication. So in order to perform the actual authentication, this authentication manager, it is going to forward the request to the authentication providers available inside the Spring Security Framework.

There are some Spring Security Framework authentication providers available. Similarly, we can also define our own authentication providers, which we're going to discuss in the coming sections. So a project can have more than one authentication provider. So the responsibility of Authentication Manager is to check with all the applicable authentication providers to identify whether the authentication is successful or failed. So once these authentication providers receive the authentication object to perform the actual authentication, these authentication providers, they're going to take help from two other components like UserDetailsManager or UserDetailsService.

Along with these UserDetailsManager is also going to take help from the Password Encoder component. Think like one of the authentication provider, it received a request in the form of authentication object. So the very first activity that my authentication provider it has to do is it has to load the user details based upon the username result. So to load these user details, it is going to take help from the UserDetailsManager or UserDetailsService implementation classes.

So once the user details are loaded, the user details will be sent back to the authentication provider. But my authentication provider, it won't compare the password provided by the user and what is present inside the storage system like database or inside the memory. It can't do the password comparison by itself. It has to take the help from another component which is Password Encoder. So this Password Encoder component is a specialist while dealing with the password comparison.

Using these Password Encoder, we can store the password using plain text or we can store them using the hashing algorithms. So since these Password Encoder is a specialist, the authentication provider will ask the Password Encoder to compare the user provided password with the password loaded from the storage system with the help of UserDetailsManager. Once the Password Encoder says that, okay, the passwords are matching accordingly, the Authentication Provider conveys back to the authentication manager saying that the authentication is successful.

So how it is going to convey that? This time inside the response, the authentication object, it is going to have the boolean value, which is isAuthenticated as true. So based upon this value, my authentication manager know whether the authentication is successful or not. The same authentication object will send back to the Spring Security filters. So now my Spring Security filters, they know whether the authentication is successful or not. Regardless of whether the authentication is successful or not, they're going to store the authentication details in a security context.

So they will store these authentication object against a session ID which is created for a given browser. So if the user is trying to access the same protected page from the same browser based upon the given session ID the Spring Security filters, they're going to load the authentication object details from the security context and accordingly, they're going to show either successful message or a error message. So this should also give a confirmation to you all the actual authentication execution is only going to happen for the very first request because there is no entry for a given session ID inside the security context.

Once the first request is processed and there is an entry inside the security context for recession ID from next time onwards, the security filters, they're not going to invoke the authentication manager. Instead they're going to leverage the details present inside the security context to send the successful response or to send an error response. At last, in the step 10, we are going to send a response to the client application. So in the scenario of authentication is successful, the client applications that are going to get a response from the REST API, otherwise if the authentication is failed, then obviously they're going to get 401 or 403 error.

LECTURE 1.12: Sequence flow of the Spring Security default behaviour
----------------------------------------

Instructor: In the previous lecture, we discussed about the internal flow of the Spring Security framework. Inside this lecture, I want to show you the sequence flow that we have discussed so far so that this sequence flow, it is going to be with you as a reference in future for any questions. You can see there are multiple important parties. The very first one is client, followed by Spring Security Filters, Authentication Manager, Authentication Provider, and User Details Manager, or User Details Service followed by Password Encoder.

So these are all the important components involved. In the very first step, the end user, he will try to access a secure page for the very first time without entering any credentials. Without what is going to happen behind the scenes, filters like Authorization Filter, Abstract Authentication Processing Filter, and DefaultLoginPageGeneratingFilter, they all going to work together and display a login page to the end user to enter the credentials.

Once the end user entered his username and password, the details will be processed again by the Spring Security filter. This time, the filters like UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter is going to extract the credentials from the request and populate the authentication object. The populated authentication object is going to be provided as an input to the AuthenticationManager implementation, which is ProviderManager. So inside this ProviderManager, we have an authenticate() method.

The same is going to be invoked, and internally this ProviderManager, it is going to iterate all the applicable authentication providers. In our scenario, the AuthenticationProvider, which is going to be invoked is DaoAuthenticationProvider. So inside this DaoAuthenticationProvider also, there is a authenticate() method. The same authenticate() method is going to be invoked by the ProviderManager. So the AuthenticationProviderImplementation, it can't authenticate the user by itself.

It is going to take help from two other components, which are InMemoryUserDetailsManager, which is the implementation of the UserDetailsManager class, and PasswordEncoder to validate the password. So basically, first it will try to load the user details from the memory with the help of these InMemoryUserDetailsManager. Post that with the help of these PasswordEncoder, it will try to validate whether the passwords are matching. If the passwords are matching, the successful authentication details is going to be returned back to the ProviderManager.

From ProviderManager, it will reach to the security filters and at last, the security filters, they are going to store the successful authentication details inside the security context object for future use. Once these details are stored at the end, the rest API response will be returned back to the end user. So here you may have a question, which is nowhere we are invoking the rest API, which is welcome, so don't worry about that. The Spring Security framework remembers what is the API that end user is trying to invoke.

If all the authentication is successful, it is going to invoke the rest API, and the response is going to send back to the filters of the Spring Security framework, which will send back to the client application. Have this sequence flow for your reference. I also have an high level sequence flow, which is another flavor of whatever we discussed so far. If you feel the previous slide has some too much information, or it is too much cluttered, then use this sequence flow.

So this also has the same kind of details but with a different style of representation. So first filters from filters, Authentication object will be populated, followed by ProviderManager, followed by AuthenticationProvider, followed by UserDetailsManager, and PasswordEncoder. The same will come back eventually to the client. I hope you like these sequence flows. Like I said previously, we are going to revisit all the internal working of the Spring Security framework at regular intervals of time based upon the new configurations we are exploring throughout the course.

And in the same process, I'm also going to update these sequence flows and provide you the updated slides as well. Thank you, and I'll catch you in the next lecture. Bye.

Right now the value started with 273. So let me click on the sign in button. And you can see, we got a new JSESSIONID value. To this JSESSIONID value, behind the scenes, Spring Security will map to a successful authenticated session where my authentication details, they're going to be stored and they'll be reloaded and reused every time when I try to access a protected API. This way, Spring Security framework, also doing a smart job of not invoking the actual authentication every time.

If you try to invoke the actual authentication for each and every request, then definitely it is going to have some performance impact. But by using this JSESSIONID cookie, the Spring Security framework is doing a smart job here. off course, I also want to highlight, this is the default behavior of the Spring Security framework. There are better and advanced approaches also available, like JWT tokens, OAuth2.0 framework, OpenID framework. So all these advanced topics we're going to explore throughout this course.

As of now, inside this section, we just built a very basic application and I just gave the quick introduction about the Spring Security framework, how the internal flow works. But more and more we are going to discuss in the coming sections. Slowly, section by section, we are going to enhance our application. And in the same process, I'm going to teach you all the approaches available inside the Spring Security framework. Before I try to close this lecture, I want to highlight you that every section code I'm going to upload into this GitHub repo, the same GitHub repo I have highlighted at the starting of the course.

Once you open this GitHub repo, you can go to the section1 to find the section1 related code. So please refer to the same code for any questions. LECTURE 3.2: Configuring PasswordEncoder using PasswordEncoderFactories
----------------------------------------

Instructor: We have two different problems with the code that we have returned in the previous lecture. The very first problem, is we're directly hard-coding the credentials inside the source code. If anyone has access to your source code, for example, if they have access to your GitHub repo, they'll be able to easily see what is the password. Username, that's fine, we can hard-code, but at least the password, we should never hard-code inside the source code.

Because with this password, anyone who have access to your code, they should be able to access your secured APIs. Off course, we're not going to use this approach for production applications. Even for that demo applications, or lower-severity applications that you're going to build with this approach, you may have a requirement, which is no one should know the password except you, or the persons with whom you have shared the password. So that's a first problem.

And the second problem is right now, the password is being stored as a plain text internally inside the application memory as well. If some hacker has access to your application heap dump, the hacker can easily get what is the password by just analyzing the heap dump. Because the credentials are stored in a plain text format. In order to solve these two problems, we need to tell to the Spring Security framework that "Please use the PasswordEncoder to store my passwords in an encrypted, or in an hashing format."

So there is a dedicated section for the PasswordEncoders, which we're going to discuss in the coming sections. But now let's try to discuss about PasswordEncoders on a high level. There are many other implementations available inside the Spring Security framework, which we're going to explore in few seconds.

So the method name I'm going to mention as PasswordEncoder only and this method also is not going to accept any input. And this is going to simply return the object of PasswordEncoder. So let's try to open this interface and try to see all the implementation classes. You can see there are good amount of implementation classes.

Most of the PasswordEncoders, they are deprecated. Because right now, they are not considered secured. These deprecated PasswordEncoders, they released very long back. So if you try to open these createDelegatingPasswordEncoder, you'll be able to see all the PasswordEncoders supported by the Spring Security framework. So there is an LdapShaPpasswordEncoder, BCryptPasswordEncoder, NoOpPasswordEncoder, SCryptPasswordEncoder. So there are good amount of PasswordEncoders that are available inside this method. Basically what Spring Security team they have done inside this method is they considered BCryptPasswordEncoder as a default PasswordEncoder.

That means they are recommending to use the BCryptPasswordEncoder as a default PasswordEncoder, even inside the production applications. Because as of today, when we use this PasswordEncoder, we can safely assume that that our passwords, they're going to be safely stored inside a storage system. It can be in-memory storage system, or database storage system, or it can be any other storage system. But all our passwords, they're not going to be stored in a plain text password.

Since we are using this method to declare the bean of PasswordEncoder, what is going to happen is if I don't mention any prefix before my password, then this password, it is going to be stored in a bcrypt hash format behind the scenes. What is a hashing and all, we are going to discuss in the coming sections. For now, please note that whenever I'm saying hashing, it is a format where your password is going to be encrypted or converted. So from these encrypted or hashed password, no one should be able to reverse the plain text password.

It's only one way. Even if the hacker holds the hash password, the hacker can't get the plain text password from the hashed password. So with that, we solved one problem. But for some reason if you're looking to use some other implementation of PasswordEncoder for example, if you don't want to use any PasswordEncoder, like you are looking for an option to store your credentials in a plain text format, then you can have this prefix which is noop.

As of now, you can see we are using noop. That's why our credentials are getting stored in the plain text format. Similarly, if you try to use any other prefix like scrypt, then in this scenario, this PasswordEncoder is going to be used to hash your password and to validate your password during the login operation. Don't get confused with all these options. Always go with the default PasswordEncoder recommended by the Spring Security team. So as of now, you can see the default PasswordEncoder that they're recommending is BCryptPasswordEncoder.

And here, you may have a question, which is instead of using this factor() method, why can't we directly create the object of BCryptPasswordEncoder? But think of a scenario where right now, this is the default recommended approach. For them also, in order to make this code work, you need to use this PasswordEncoderFactories. So the legacy application, they're going to configure their users with the prefix of MD4, whereas you're going to configure your user details with the prefix of bcrypt. This way, we are going to have an option either to follow the default BCryptPasswordEncoder, or if we mention these in the prefix value, then the corresponding PasswordEncoders, they're going to be considered at the runtime for validation of the password and for storing of the password.

LECTURE 3.4: Deep Dive of UserDetailsService & UserDetailsManager Interfaces
----------------------------------------

Instructor: Long back, we discussed the Spring Security internal flow. I hope you remember this internal flow. Inside this internal flow, like you can see, the Authentication Providers, they're going to leverage two different components to actually perform the authentication. By now, I'm assuming you are clear about the role of Password Encoder and UserDetailsManager or UserDetailsService. But you may have some confusion. What is a UserDetailsManager and what is a UserDetailsService?

Under which scenarios we need to use the UserDetailsService and under which scenario we need to use the UserDetailsManager? If you have any confusion around Password Encoder, don't worry. There is a separate section where we are going to talk everything about password encoders, hashing. In the same section, you are going to get clarity around the password encoder. For now, let's try to concentrate on this component, which is UserDetailsManager or UserDetailsService.

This is the slide that I have prepared to clear your confusion around the UserDetailsManager and UserDetailsService interfaces and its implementation classes. So for the next few lectures, we are going to discuss everything around the user management related important classes and interfaces available inside the Spring Security framework. At the very top, we have an interface, which is UserDetailsService. Inside this interface, there is going to be a Single Abstract Method, which is going to load the user details from any storage system.

It can be an in-memory storage system or it can be a database. Regardless of whatever is a storage system, the purpose of this method is to load the user details from a storage system based upon a given username. Now this interface is extended by another interface which is UserDetailsManager. So this UserDetailsManager has many other abstract methods. The very first one is createUser(), which is going to create a new user based upon the object that we're trying to provide as an input.

The type of the object that we need to provide for these methods is UserDetails. So basically, whenever we try to create a new user or whenever we are trying to register a new account, this is the method which is going to be used by the Spring Security framework to create the UserDetails inside the storage system. Next, in the scenarios where the end user want to update his or her details. In such scenarios, the updateUser() method is going to come into picture followed by deleteUser() method, which is going to delete the user details from the storage system based upon the username that we are trying to provide as an input.

But in the scenarios where the end user simply want to change the password. In such scenarios, instead of using the updateUser(), we are going to use the changePassword() method. So this is going to accept what is a old password and what is a new password. And at last, there is also a helper method available inside this interface which is userExists(). So for example, if someone want to understand if there is an user available inside a storage system based upon a given username before actually performing any authentication, then they can use this method.

Here, you may have a question which is, why there is a separation of UserDetailsService and UserDetailsManager? So there is a very good reason why Spring Security team, they separated these methods into two different interfaces. The very first interface that we see on the top is UserDetailsService. The reason why these interface has method which is going to help only the load user details by username is sometimes organizations, they simply always want to authenticate the user.

They never have a scenario where the end user is going to come and directly register using their website or using their APIs. So if they don't have a scenario of creating the user, deleting the user or updating the user, they can simply go with the UserDetailsService implementation alone. So the implementation class of this interface, it is always going to read the user details. So when we are going to read the user details? During the login attempt.

There'll be some organizations where they will give some credentials to the end user and they want them to use those credentials always during the login. They will not give flexibility to restart a new account or to update the details or to change the password. So for such organizations, having an implementation class for this interface alone is going to be sufficient. But coming to the scenarios where if an organization want to have complete functionality of user details like creating, updating, deleting, reading, changing the password, checking if the user is exist, in such scenarios, they can build an implementation of this UserDetailsManager.

So basically this UserDetailsManager, it is going to support all the CRUD operations. C means create, R means read. So this read functionality is going to get from the parent interface, and U means update, and D means delete. With this, it should be very clear for you if an organization is looking for an option to provide all the CRUD operations options to the end user, then they have to implement the UserDetailsManager interface. Otherwise, if they're just looking to authenticate end user, they need to implement the UserDetailsService interface.

So these are the interfaces or the contracts provided by the Spring Security that we need to follow whenever we are dealing with the user details inside the storage system. But the beauty of the Spring Security is, the team didn't sit ideal by just providing the contract or by just providing the interfaces. Instead, they provided some sample implementation classes as well. For example, InMemoryUserDetailsManager is the implementation class of this UserDetailsManager.

We saw previously whenever we want to create the users inside the memory of the application, we can happily use these implementation class. We explored this class a lot in the previous lectures since this is a very common requirement for many organizations who are getting started around Spring Security. What Spring Security team has done, is behind the scenes, they have provided these InMemoryUserDetailsManager, which is an implementation of UserDetailsManager inside the library itself.

The next two common requirement people may have is, to store the user details inside the database. To handle the scenarios where the user details are stored inside the database, we have one implementation class provided by the Spring Security, which is JdbcUserDetailsManager. Apart from JDBC and InMemory, one more common approach to store the user details is LDAP. So LDAP is one of the legacy style of storing the UserDetails inside a storage system.

Not many companies that are going to use this LDAP system, but if some organization, they're using these LDAP storage system, then they can happily leverage the LdapUserDetailsManager provided by the Spring Security team. For some reason, if all these three options they are not helping you, then you can implement your own custom UserDetailsManager, you're always welcome to build your own custom UserDetailsManager. We are going to explore the option of building our own custom implementation in the upcoming sections.

For now, I'm assuming you are clear about the role of all these three layers. The very first layer, which is an interface, is UserDetailsService followed by another interface, which is UserDetailsManager, followed by three different implementation classes provided by the Spring Security team. And at the end, you might have seen this green arrow, which indicates the UserDetails interface. The beauty of all this contract, which is provided by the Spring Security team is, they all leverage these UserDetails interface.

Inside Spring Security, a user is represented by UserDetails. So UserDetails is an interface which represent an end user, like what username, what credentials, what authorities the end user is going to have. But before that, let me pass the input parameter to this method, which is going to be email. So here we are just declaring the abstract method and you may have a question which is where is the implementation logic? That's the beauty of spring data JPA. We don't have to write the implementation logic. At the runtime, the JPA framework, it is going to generate the required logic to fetch the customer record based upon the email. There is a method naming standard that you need to follow inside the Spring Data JPA.

If you follow that method naming standard, the JPA can understand what you are trying to convey. So inside the JPA, whenever we are using, findBy(), it means I'm trying to select the data or I'm trying to read the data. Post that I have mentioned the column name, which is, Email. SECTION 5: Password Management with PasswordEncoders

----------------------------------------
LECTURE 5.1: How our passwords validated with out PasswordEncoders
----------------------------------------

Instructor: Inside the previous section, we have created a new REST API with the name register. And with the help of this registered API, we're able to create and store the end user details inside the database. Here I want to explain you about one interesting point, which is if you see here inside this API, we're trying to send this as a request and the password we're trying to send is a plain text password. In real applications, if an end user is trying to use an UI application to register himself, then even in UI scenario also, the end user is always going to enter the password using plain text only.

But by the time we are trying to store these user details inside the database, the password value is getting hashed with a Bcrypto PasswordEncoder. And with that, we are following a production recommended standard, which is know where we are trying to store the plain text password. But you may have multiple questions here, which is I didn't tell anything to my Spring Security framework to encrypt with the help of BcryptPasswordEncoder. Why it is selecting only the BcryptPasswordEncoder and where this hashing of the password is happening?

The answer is very simple. Inside our User controller class where we have this registerUser() method, here, we're trying to use the encode() method of the PasswordEncoder. So this method is responsible to convert the plain text password into a hash password. I hope your one question is resolved. Now moving on to the next question. Where do we define that we have to use the Bcrypt PasswordEncoder? This can be your second question. The answer is very simple.

We discussed long back around this. So let me go to the ProjectSecurityConfig and here you'll be able to see we are using the password encoder factories to create the bean of PasswordEncoder. If you try to open this method, you'll be able to see there are multiple PasswordEncoders available throughout the Spring Security framework, but by default, the Spring Security framework is going to use the bcrypt password encoder. That's why in this method they hardcoded the encoding ID as bcrypt.

So whatever hardcoded value you see here, the same you can assume as the default PasswordEncode being used by the Spring Security framework. And this may change in the future based upon the advancements happening. But right now this is the default password encoder. That's why though we're not sending any prefix inside the request that we are trying to send, still, behind the scenes, the Spring Security is taking care of using the default password encoder and append these prefix value to the password hash value before it try to save into the database.

So with this, what is going to happen is in future when now this John is trying to log in through the login page or through any other mechanism, John is simply going to enter his plain text password. So this kind of validation is going to happen behind the scenes by the Spring Security when it is trying to compare the user entered password with the hash password stored inside the database. We can also directly create the bean of Bcrypt PasswordEncoder here instead of using this. But with that we will end up always using the Bcrypt PasswordEncoder. And in future, if there are some advancements happening, you need to come and make some changes inside your code.

But with this createDelegatingPasswordEncoder() method, we don't have worry about which PasswordEncoder object I need to consider to create the bean. So all such tensions we can hand over to the Spring Security framework and we can happily sleep. Behind the scenes, Spring Security framework is going to consider all the prefix values mentioned here. So based upon these prefix values, it is going to select the corresponding password encoder. For example, think like maybe you have a legacy application where they have the password stored with the help of prefix MD5.

Throughout this section we're going to talk lot details about how to manage the passwords with the help of PasswordEncoder. Otherwise we know what is going to happen. Always developers will try to store the passwords using plain text format. LECTURE 5.3: What is Encryption, Decryption & why it is not suitable for passwords management
----------------------------------------

Instructor: Most of developers, they assume encryption is the right option for the passwords management. If you're under the same assumption, you are wrong, encryption is not the right option. Let's try to understand why encryption is not the right option for the passwords management. What is encryption? Encryption is a process of transforming data in such a way that guarantees confidentiality. How this confidentiality is going to be assured? Whenever someone is trying to encrypt a plain text value, they're going to use a secret along with the encryption algorithm.

In cryptographic terminology, we call these secret as key. Once the encryption is completed, it can only be reversed by using the same algorithm, and the same secret key. As long as someone take care of securing their secret key and make sure that no unauthorized person can get this key, then we can assume that encryption is a safety process. But still, this is not a recommended approach for passwords management because some person has to generate the secret key, as some application has to generate the secret key very first time during the encryption process.

If the person or if the application, which is trying to generate the secret key, if they lose the secret key, then there is no security or confidentiality in the encryption process. Let's try to understand more details about encryption. Like you can see inside this visual diagram, whenever we have a plain text password, we can apply the encryption along with the secret key, and with that we are going to get an encrypted text. So this encrypted text, in other words, we can also call it as cipher text.

So this encrypted or cipher text can only be decrypted to the plain text using the same secret key. Without that same secret key decryption is not possible. So based upon how these key is being maintained inside the encryption and decryption process, the encryption is categorized into two types. The very first type of encryption is symmetric, and the other type is asymmetric encryption. We know inside the encryption, there is going to be an algorithm along with the secret key.

There are multiple encryption algorithms available inside the industry. So whatever algorithm you are trying to use as part of the encryption, the same algorithm has to be used during that decryption process as well. Now, coming to the key, the key can be managed in two different ways, one is symmetric, and the other one is asymmetric. So let's try to understand what are these two types of encryptions. In the very first type of encryption, which is symmetric encryption, we are going to use the same secret key during the encryption and decryption process.

So you can see here, I have the plain text to value, and to this I'm going to apply some encryption algorithm along with the secret key. With that, I'm going to get a cipher text as an output. Now, if I want to decrypt the cipher text to the plain text value, I need to use the same encryption algorithm. At the same time, I'm also going to use the same secret key. Since we are using the same secret key for the encryption and decryption, this type of encryption, we call them as symmetric encryption.

There is a drawback with the symmetric encryption, though it is trying to provide the confidentiality, if someone lose the secret key to unauthorized persons, then they should be able to do both encryption and decryption. That's why in this scenario, the strength of your encryption depends upon how strongly you are protecting your secret key. Think of a scenario, there is an application, and it want to communicate with various third party applications.

Like there is an application with one, two, three, and four. Since this application A want to communicate with the help of symmetric encryption with all the other third party applications, what it is going to do is it's going to communicate with all these third parties saying that, "Let's try to use a secret key for the encryption and decryption process." Let's assume the secret key value is one, two, three. So the same is distributed for all the third party apps, and the same also being maintained inside the application as well.

Though this application A make sure that this key is well secured, we can't guarantee if the other third party applications, if they have stored and using the secret key for good purposes. If there is a scenario where one of the third party application loses the secret key, there is a very good chance that entire encryption process may get compromised. That's why symmetric encryption is only used in the scenarios where you are trying to encrypt the data in rest or data at rest.

So what is data at rest? Let's take the example of AWS S3 buckets. So inside AWS S3 buckets, we can store any amount of data, it can be logs, or it can be images, videos. You can store any kind of data inside these S3 buckets. AWS, it is going to give an option to their customers if they want to encrypt that data at rest, which is being stored inside the S3 buckets. If the organizations enroll for the encryption, then in this scenario, what AWS is going to do behind the scenes is whenever a new data is being stored into the S3 buckets, it is going to encrypt the data with the secret key, which is known only to the AWS.

AWS is also going to give you an option if you want to provide your own secret key. With that, even if someone get handhold onto the data, which is present inside the S3 buckets, it is going to be useless for them because the data is encrypted and they can't get the secret key either from the AWS or either from the organization. And whenever the organization is trying to read the data from these S3 buckets, AWS behind the scenes, it is going to decrypt the data using the secret key and send the data in a plain format to the organization who owns the data.

So please, make sure you are using the symmetric encryption only in the scenarios of data in rest or data at rest. And, to some extent, you can also use the symmetric encryption if there is only a single application use involved. Don't try to use a symmetric encryption if there are multiple parties involved during the encryption and decryption process. Even if one of the third party application is compromised, then your encryption is going to be useless.

I hope you're clear about what is symmetric encryption. Let's go to the asymmetric encryption. Inside asymmetric encryption, we are going to have two different keys. The very first one is public key, the other one is private key. Whenever someone want to initiate the encryption process, what they are going to do is the owner who is trying to initiate the whole encryption process, they are going to generate two types of keys. The very first one is public key, and the second one is private key.

The owner, they will keep the private key with themself, and they will distribute the public key to any number of third party applications. So whoever has this public key, they will be able to perform only the encryption. So once this encryption is completed, the cipher text is going to be received by the owner who initiated all this encryption process. So the owner during the decryption, they have to use the private key to decrypt the data to plain text.

They can't use a public key for the decryption process. That means anyone can generate the encrypted data with the public key, but the decryption process can be done only by the owner who owns the private key. So this is one style of encryption. Since there are two different types of keys are being used here, we call this approach as asymmetric encryption. This asymmetric encryption is ideal for encrypting the data in transit. Let's try to understand what do I mean by data in transit.

Think of a scenario, there is an application A, and application B. This application A, it want to fetch some data from the application B, it want to read data, but the application A want to read the data only in the encrypted format because application A is very scared that someone may steal the data in between the network. So that's why in this scenario, what application A is going to do is it is going to generate a public key and private key. And this public key, it is going to send to the application B to use it during the encryption process.

So using the public key provided by the application A, the application B, it is going to perform the encryption. Once the encryption is completed, encrypted data will be sent back to the application A. So now think of a scenario, someone in the middle, they hack the data. For them, this encrypted data is not going to make any sense because they don't have the private key to decrypt the data. So who can decrypt this data? It can be only done by application A because it holds the private key.

So this way, both application A and B, they communicated with each other with the help of asymmetric encryption. With all the discussion that we have done so far, you might be under the assumption that "Why can't we use encryption for passwords management? Our application can make sure that no one is stealing the secret key," that can be your assumption, but in reality, it is not going to work that way. You may have people inside your organization only who is looking to steal your secret key.

That's why though these encryption option is providing confidentiality option, it is not providing the integrity option. You can't guarantee that no one can steal you a secret keys or private keys. If someone steals your keys, then all the encrypted data can be easily decrypted by them. That's why we should also not consider the encryption process for the password management. I hope you're clear about the encryption. In the next lecture, let's see the small demo of encryption.

Thank you, bye.

LECTURE 5.5: Introduction to Hashing
----------------------------------------

Instructor: We discussed everything about the encoding and encryption, and in the same process, we also concluded that both encoding and encryption, they are not suitable for the passwords management. With that, we left with the winner, which is hashing. If anyone ask you how you are trying to store the passwords inside the database, you should tell them that you are leveraging the hashing mechanism to store the password securely inside the database.

In simple words, we can say hashing is a process where data is converted into a hash value or a digest value using some mathematical hashing function.

So behind the scenes, whenever you try to provide a plain text to the hash function, it is going to execute some mathematical calculations with the help of the hashing function, and it is going to provide you an output value. This output value, we call it as hash value or digest value. The beauty of the hashing process is data once hashed, it is going to be non-reversible. No one can determine what is the original data by using a hash value that got generated initially.

So you may have a lot many questions. So let's try to deep dive into the hashing and try to understand the same step by step. First, I want to make you clear that hashing is always one way. You can see, we can provide the plain text to the hash function, and we are going to get a digest or hash value as an output. So from this hash, we can't derive the text value, so this is not possible. There is no reversing process for the hash function. One more beauty of hashing is we know hashing always going to give you some hash value based upon your input text value.

For 12345, this is how the hash value is going to look like. So based upon what type of hash function you are trying to use, accordingly, the output is going to vary. The beauty of hashing is, if you give the same plain text value to the same hash function, you're always going to get the same hash value. Regardless, you are trying to invoke the hash function 100 times or 1,000 times, hashing is always going to give the same output value. This is very important.

The same kind of feature we also observe for encoding and encryption. There are many other features which makes hashing a beautiful concept. Let's try to understand one by one. Whenever you use the hashing, regardless of whatever amount of data that you're trying to as an input, you're always going to get a fixed set of hash value. Here I'm trying to give 12345 as a input, and this is how the hash value is going to look like. I'm talking about the length but not the content. For example, if you use the SHA-256 hashing function, you're always going to get the output hash value with the 256 bits. Whenever you are thinking about hashing, always remember the blenders that we use on our day-to-day life. Let's try to understand why I'm trying to compare hashing with the blender. To the blenders, think like you're trying to give the input, which are fruits. So if you try to provide these fruits as the input to the blender, you are going to get juice as an output.

Now, if I give the same juice to the blender back, will I get the fruits? Off course not, because it is irreversible process. The same property applies for hashing also, so hashing is always one way. So due to these characters of the hashing, hashing is majorly used in the password management, and apart from that, wherever we need the integrity of the data in such scenarios, also hashing is getting used to a great extent. Instructor: Inside this lecture, let's try to understand how to overcome the drawbacks of hashing so that we can use hashing with 100% confidence inside the passwords management. These drawbacks of hashing can be overcomed by following two different solutions. Both of these solutions has to be used by all the organizations to improve the strength of their hashing process. The very first process is they should use the salts during the password hashing.

Now, this salt will be added to the password, which is 12345. So this is going to be the total value. This total value will be given to the hash function to derive an hash value. For example, think like the hash value is calculated as aef4c. It just a random value I'm trying to give. It's a simple value I'm trying to give here. So the salt value is aex2fdac. So this salt value, they can store either in a plain text value or they can encode it or they can encrypt it. It's up to them how they want to store the salt value. So please note that this is that total hash value for the combination of salt and password. Along with the hash value, they will also store the what is the salt they have used during the hashing process. So this is the total value that is going to be stored into the database.

What is advantage that we are getting if we try to add the random salt value? The purpose of adding these random salt value is, even if one of the other user has the same password, which is 12345, for him, the salt value is going to be different.

Though the password is same, the overall hash value is going to be the different value. The reason is the salt value, which is going to be randomly generated for each and every user. With this, each and every user inside your database, they are going to have their own unique hash value. Their passwords can be same, but their hash value is going to be unique because due to the different salt values we're trying to use. Now, with this, let's try to understand how the problem of rainbow attacks or dictionary attack and brute force attack is going to be solved.

The reason is very simple. He will only have the hash values for the plain text passwords are for the simple passwords. He can't guess the what is the random salt value that each user is going to have before the data breach. The purpose of these tables is he's going to prepare these tables before the data breach itself so that his job of cracking the password is going to be fast.

But with the salt value that we are going to add for each and every user, though he have these dictionary or rainbow tables prepared, he can't use them. These tables are going to be useless because the hacker can never know what is the salt that we are going to add to these 12345. Maybe he will come to know once the data breach has happen and once the hacker checks the database value where we are storing the salt to place hash value. So with this, these attacks we are trying to avoid.

He will keep on trying some random passwords or some simple passwords, which is 12345, or any other simple passwords, or he will keep on going to try various passwords using the UI application or using whatever mechanism that application is going to expose.

In this scenario, the salt is not going to protect us because during the login operation, the backend API, it is going to derive the salt value from the value that we stored inside the database column and up into the value entered by the hacker inside the UI application. Think one of the scenario where the hacker gets the user1 password, which is 12345 correctly, and he entered this password onto the UI. And behind the scenes, the backend is going to leverage the salt value and up into this user-entered value, and it is going to generate the overall hash value and the hash is going to match.

Here, the salt is not protecting from the brute force attack. So to avoid these kind of brute force scenarios, organizations, they are going to have various approaches. The very first approach is as soon as they detect someone entered three consecutive invalid passwords, they are going to lock the account. So you might have observed this kind of thing in many of the websites. So with this, the hacker is going to have only three attempts to guess the password.

So we are trying to limit the hacker options here. The next option is websites, they will not accept the simple passwords during the registration process. They will expect the end user to use at least eight characters as the passwords, with a combination of numbers, letters, and special characters. So with this, the end users will end up picking up some strong password, but not the simple passwords like 12345 or password. So all these kind of simple password, they can't use, because the organizations, they are enforced these rules during the registration process.

This way, the organizations, they are going to avoid the brute force attack. So this is scenario one of brute force attack. The second scenario is, think like the hacker steal all the data present inside your organization DB. It has all the hash values of the all the users. So for user1, think like the hash value stored inside the database is salt plus overall hash value. So this is the value stored inside the database. So from this value, the hacker easily will know what is the salt value, he just have to guess the what is the original password.

So in this scenario, the salt is not protecting us. So there is one more solution which we need to implement to protect from these kind of scenarios. Before I try to explain that solution, let's try to think what is going to happen whenever hacker is trying to guess some password. So for each combination, he has to follow the process of what is a guessed password. So I'll just mention G here, guessed password, and plus salt value that he get from the database.

So the total hash value, he will try to compare with this. So this operation, he has to perform for all the millions of guesses or thousands of guesses he's going to do. And this is not going to be a problem for him because the hash function is super fast. He can try to guess all the combinations by taking some one week time or by taking some one month time because the hash functions are very fast. So to overcome this challenge, we need to make the hash functions intentionally slower.

By default, the hash functions are fast, we know that, but to fix this issue, we need to make it slow. So how to make these hash functions slow? It's very easy. Inside the industry, there are some password encoders or password hashing algorithms. We need to use those algorithms only, hashing algorithms. For example, Bcrypt is one such algorithm, and Script is another algorithm, and Argon2 is another algorithm. So these are all the password hashing algorithms or the password encoders that industry recommends.

So when we use these hashing algorithms, so what is going to happen is they are going to intentionally slow the process of hashing. For example, for each hashing that you want to perform, they are going to take intentionally one second. So previously, if you try to use a simple hashing passwords, the hashing is going to complete within millisecond or nanoseconds, but right now, we slow them by bringing two seconds. If needed, we can tune these algorithms to slow the hashing process for two seconds or three seconds based upon your business requirements.

Apart from the slowing the hashing process, these password hashing algorithms, they are going to demand lot of CPU time and they also require lot of RAM memory time. So they're going to make the hashing process more complicated. So with this setup of slow hashing algorithms, for any hacker to guess a password, it is going to take at least 10 years. For example, think like one of the organization enforced to use least eight characters as a password, with the combination of upper case value, lower case value, numbers, and special characters.

So with this combination, if someone choose a password, to guess these password with the slow hashing algorithms, for the hacker, it's going to take a lot of time. Apart from time, the hacker also should invest millions of dollars to provide the CPU time and RAM memory for the hashing algorithms. So this is how we are going to prevent the second scenario of brute force attack where the hacker already know what is the hash value. I hope you are getting these explanation.

But here, you may have some interesting question, which is, if we are intentionally slowing the hashing algorithms by following these password hashing algorithms, then can't it affect as also the same way? This can be your question. No, it is not going to affect the organization the same way. For example, think like one of the user, how many times he's going to register in his lifetime? He's going to register only one time. That means for a single user, we need to spend one second time, and we should provide some CPU time and RAM memory.

And later on, during the login, also the end user, he's not going to log in every second or every minute. Maybe he may log in into the application the same login session he may use for next one hour or for next two hours or throughout the day. That's why providing these RAM memory, CPU memory, or one second time during the login or during the registration process is not going to affect the organizations because the end user can wait for one second to log in into his application.

It's not going to give any bad experience. So what are the solutions that we need to follow to overcome all the drawbacks? We need to make our hashing algorithms slow. So this is one of the solution. And the second solution is, we need to make sure we are generating the random salt values during the registration process. The same salt values we should also store inside the database. I'm assuming you'll not have such requirements for production applications. The next password encoder that I want to discuss is StandardPasswordEncoder. This used to be a secured password encoder, maybe if we get back, people might have accept these hashing algorithm, but right now, no one accept these as a strong hashing algorithm, because due to the advancements happened inside the CPU and GPU systems, hackers can easily crack the password by using methods like Brute force attack. In other words, whenever someone uses this hashing algorithm today, it is not going to make the hashing process slow enough for the hackers to not crack the password.

Next, let's go to the password encoder, which is Pbkdf2PasswordEncoder. This password encoder can also be used by the organizations, and this is not a deprecated password encoder. Let's try to understand how this PasswordEncoder is going to work. So, this PasswordEncoder is an implementation of PBKDF2. This PasswordEncoder is going to support to configure a random salt value of length 16 bytes. So, we can have the salt value up to 16 bytes. Apart from salt, we can also configure number of iterations that the hashing has to be performed.

The default iteration value is 310000, or 310k. You may have a question, which is, what is the purpose of this iteration? Based upon this iteration value, the hashing mechanism is going to be iterated so many times. So, if you mention the iteration as 10, then the hashing process is going to be iterated 10 different times. For example, first it will try to hash a value, by taking that first hash value, it is going to perform one more iteration to bring the second hash value.

So this way, it is going to keep on iterating based upon the configured iterations to derive the final hash value. This is how the hashing algorithms, they're going to slow the hashing process. If one logic is going to be executed with this number of iterations, then obviously the overall output is going to be delayed by few seconds. The specialty of this password and quota is, whatever secret that you have configured, it can be further tuned based upon the function that you are going to pass.

So you can see here, the third point says, a configurable key derivation function. So, if you try to look into this class, you'll be able to see certain constants, which is default salt length is equal to 16, and what is a default algorithm to use to derive the new key based upon the secret provided by the developer, and what is a DEFAULT_HASH_WIDTH, and what are the DEFAULT_ITERATIONS?

If you can scroll down, you'll be able to see the logic present inside the encode() method. So, let me go to the encode() method. Spring Security Team also recommends using this BCryptPasswordEncoder.

So, it has three different versions, like 2a, 2b, 2y, we can either configure a specific version of this hashing algorithm, or we can let the Spring Security to consider one of the default version. The larger the strength parameter, the more work will have to be done exponentially.

There is a default constructor, and there is a constructor which is going to accept the strength. So the strength value has to be between 4 and 31. So the minimum is 4, and the maximum can be 31. The more strength value you try to configure, the more time the hashing and the matching process is going to take. The specialty of the BCryptPasswordEncoder is it is going to demand lot of CPU computation power. This hashing algorithm, it is going to intentionally slow down the hashing process by doing multiple iterations of hashing based upon the strength that we are trying to provide.

Apart from strength, we can also provide what is the BCrypt version that we want to use, and there is also a constructor which is going to accept both a BCrypt version, and some secure random number which is going to be involved inside the hashing process. So, there are multiple constructors available which you can explore. In the scenarios where the strength is less than 4, and greater than 31, it's going to throw an exception, saying that "Bad strength." In case if no one is passing the strength in such scenarios, based upon this logic, they are setting that 10 as the default strength. So, the version, and random, they're going to be set to the version and random variables. Let's try to see what logic we have inside the encode() method. Inside the encode() method, first they're trying to generate the salt, later on, they're trying to invoke the hashpw() method, along with the rawPassword and the salt that got generated.

This BCrypt class is present inside the crypto package of Spring Security Library, so all the logic around the BCrypt hashing algorithm, you'll be able to see inside this class. Here, it is invoking the checkpw() method available inside the BCrypt by providing both the rawPassword and the encodedPassword. The actual logic of comparing both these passwords is present inside this BCrypt.java class.

Now, let's go to the SCryptPasswordEncoder. So, SCryptPasswordEncoder is an advanced version of BCryptPasswordEncoder. The specialty of SCryptPasswordEncoder is it is going to leverage the SCrypt hashing function, and whenever someone is using this hashing function, we can configure CPU cost, memory cost, and the parallelization. With these configurations, we can make hacker life tough, because the hacker has to provide the CPU computation, by having a high-end machine.

Apart from that, you should also have lot of RAM to support the memory cost, and, based upon the parallelization parameter, the hacker should also support parallelization execution, or multi-threading execution. So, with these three parameters, these SCryptPasswordEncoder considered more stronger than BCryptPasswordEncoder. I'll come to the point that why Spring Security team are recommending to use a BCryptPasswordEncoder. The next PasswordEncoder we have is Argon2PasswordEncoder.

So, a few years back, there is a competition happened in the industry to identify which hashing algorithm is the winner. In that competition, the winner is Argon2. Argon2 hashing algorithm is the latest hashing algorithm, which is an advanced version of SCrypt hashing algorithm. This also allow you to configure CPU cost, memory cost, and parallelization parameter. The way that SCrypt and Argon2 work, it is almost similar, just that Argon2 is the latest version, and it handles the drawbacks of a SCryptPasswordEncoder.

I hope you're clear, but in real projects, as of today, most of the organizations, especially people who are using Spring Security, they are right now using the BCryptPasswordEncoder, because Spring Security team recommends to use this as the password encoder inside production applications. Now coming to the point, why can't we use the SCrypt and Argon2 compared to the BCrypt? The answer is very simple, no one is stopping you in using the SCrypt and Argon2PasswordEncoder, your authentication process is going to work very similar to the BCryptPasswordEncoder.

It's just that if you try to use the SCrypt and Argon2PasswordEncoders, the configuration is going to be more tough, because you need to right-tune the CPU cost, memory cost, parallelization cost, so you need to find a balance, or a sweet spot, which is going to work for you by making the hacker life tough. Since it needs three different parameters, like CPU cost, memory cost, and parallelization, definitely, this also going to impact your application performance during the login and registration.

So if you don't want super-slow hashing algorithm, you can use the BCryptPasswordEncoder, because it does the job, it is the recommended by Spring Security, since it is simple to use, and it also allows you to rightly balance how much slow you want to go with the hashing process. Maybe in future, due to the advancements that are going to happen in GPUs and CPUs, maybe BCrypt may get deprecated, but I think it may take five or six more years, let's not worry about it, and let's use the BCryptPasswordEncoder inside our applications.
