Instructor: Inside this new section, we're going to talk everything about the Authentication Provider in the same process. I'm also going to explain to you how to define our own Authentication Provider. As of now, we are relying on the inbuilt provided Authentication Provider, which is DaoAuthenticationProvider. This default authentication provider, it is doing a very good job. And with the help of this, we're able to perform the authentication of the end user.

But there will be certain scenarios where we may need to define our own authentication providers. I'm going to explain what are those scenarios in few minutes. Before we try to jump into the details of the authentication providers, I want to strike off these two other components that we have discussed so far. We discuss everything around the UserDetailService and UserDetailsManager along with the PasswordEncoder. So, that's why I'm trying to strike off.

During my childhood days also, I used to strike off all the chapters that I am done reading for an exam, and that is going to provide me a feeling of accomplishment. So, that's what I'm trying to do here. I hope you're also getting that feeling. Now, let's move on to the serious talking around the Authentication Providers. The very first question that you may have is the default authentication provider, which is DaoAuthenticationProvider is doing a great job and we are able to perform the authentication of the user by just loading the user details from the database with our own UserDetailsService implementation.

So, everything looks perfect. Then, why should I learn about AuthenticationProvider and under which scenario we need to provide our own custom Authentication Provider? So, this can be your question. So, let's try to understand the same by going to the next slide. As of now, we are building a very small application, but in real projects or in real enterprise applications, the security requirements may not look very simple. You may have some complex scenarios, you may have some peculiar scenarios.

So, we need to be ready for all sort of scenarios. For example, here we have a scenario where one of the enterprise application, they want to provide multiple styles of authentication. The very first style is they want to allow the end user to log in with their username and password for certain applications. And for other type of applications, they want to allow the authentication with the help of OAUTH2 framework. So, OAUTH2 is a standard which we're going to discuss in the coming sections.

It is an advanced authentication and authorization framework, which everyone uses these days. But now, please note that this is one more style of authenticating the user. And similarly the organization also have the requirement for certain applications or for certain users to authenticate them with the help of JAAS. So, what is a JASS? JAAS means Java Authentication and Authorization Service. So, inside the Java library itself, we have a small security plugin, our authentication framework, which is provided by the Java team.

Not many organizations uses this protocol these days because these days everyone's favorite is Spring Security. But you may end up in some scenarios where a certain organization may want to support login into an Legacy application with the help of this JAAS. So, based upon our discussion, it should be pretty clear for you that this organization or this scenario has a lot of complex security requirements. So for all these kind of scenarios, we need to write our own Authentication Provider implementations.

In the scenario of UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken, the Spring Security Framework should invoke the authentication provider 1, and in the scenario of who are to log in, it should invoke the authentication provider 2. And in the last scenario, it should invoke the authentication provider 3. That's what I tried to show here. So, any request that is coming towards your application, it is going to be intercepted by the filters. And these filters, they will prepare an object of authentication.

The same Authentication object is going to be provided to the AuthenticationManager. Since AuthenticationManager is an interface, we can't use it inside the authentication flow. Instead, the provider manager is going to be involved, which is the implementation of AuthenticationManager. The job of this Provider Manager is to check what is the type of authentication being performed by an end user. If the type of authentication is with the help of username and password, the provider manager should simply invoke the first authentication provider, which supports UsernamePassword authentication.

Otherwise, for the scenario two, it should invoke the OAUTH2 authentication provider. At last, if the authentication type is JAAS authentication, then ProviderManagers should invoke the third authentication provider implementation. Here you may have a question which is, "How do my ProviderManager will know which authentication provider to invoke?" That's where the beauty of Authentication object will come into picture. So, based upon the type of your Authentication object, whether it is an UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken, or whether it is a JAAS authentication token type.

So, based upon the Authentication object type, the ProviderManager is going to identify the corresponding Authentication Provider. I'm going to show you more details around this in the next lecture when we are exploring the authentication provider related code inside the framework code. Apart from supporting multiple styles of authentication, there will be some other scenarios where you may need to write down your own implementation of Authentication Provider.

Let's try to understand what are such scenarios. As of now, default Authentication Provider, which is DaoAuthenticationProvider, it is taking help of user detailed service implementation. In the previous lecture, we have implemented our own custom UserDetailsService implementation, which is EazyBankUserDetailsService class. So inside this class, we return all the code on how the user details should be loaded from the database. So with this flow, we are happy the DaoAuthenticationProvider is taking the help from the UserDetailsService implementation to just load the user details.

Once the user details are loaded from the storage system, the actual authentication of password comparison and the decision of authentication is going to happen inside the Authentication Provider. But there will be some scenarios where you may have your own custom authentication requirements. For example, think like you have a requirement to allow the authentication of an user only if the user age is greater than 18, or you may have some custom requirement where you want to allow the authentication only from certain countries.

So, if you have these kind of custom requirements and obviously the default provider, DaoAuthenticationProvider is not going to help you because whatever logic that you're going to write inside the EazyBankUserDetailsService, it is only going to help you to load the user details from the storage system. But it is not going to help you to validate the age details or country details, or any other details that are required for your custom authentication.

To accommodate these kind of requirements, you need to define your own AuthenticationProvider implementation. And inside your own AuthenticationProvider implementation, once the user details are loaded from your UserDetailsService, you can perform the additional checks like age check or country check, or any other custom checks. Once you are satisfied with these additional checks of authentication, you can create an Authentication object representing either a successful authentication or a failure authentication inside your own Authentication Provider.

Once your own Authentication Provider returns authentication object, the ProviderManager is going to take care of sending back the details to the filters, and from the filters it will go back to the end user. I hope you're clear about under which scenarios we need to consider defining our own Authentication Provider implementation. Inside the next lecture, let's try to understand more details about the Authentication Provider. Thank you, and I'll catch you in the next lecture, bye.

Using profiles inside a Spring Boot application, we can activate a specific set of properties or a specific set of beans based upon a environment. In real applications that developers, they're going to create a profile for each environment.

They're going to have a dev profile, QA profile, prod profile, SIT profile. Since they're going to create different profiles for different environments, with the help of these profiles, they will be able to control the behavior of the application by activating a specific set of properties or a specific set of bean. As of now, we just have a single property file inside our project, which is application.properties. With this Spring Boot always going to load only a single profile, which is default.

This gives a confirmation that if you're not setting up any profiles inside our application, by default the Spring Boot is going to fall back to that default profile. Inside this default to profile all the properties that we have mentioned inside the application.properties is going to be considered.

LECTURE 7.2: Exception Handling in Spring Security framework
----------------------------------------

Whenever we are trying to a secured API, a secured path, we need to make sure we are passing proper username and password. So here I'm trying to test one of the secured API with the help of Postman. Since I'm using Postman, I need to make sure I'm using the auth type as Basic Auth and I need to enter the username and password. If I try to send this request, you'll be able to see a successful response. If you use the browser, the behavior is going to be different.

You're going to see a login page and you need to enter the login credentials. But in the scenarios where if we enter the invalid credentials in the UI page, we are going to get an error message saying that the credentials are wrong. Let's try to understand what is going to happen inside the Postman. So here I'm going to give an invalid username. Password, I can't give invalid password because right now we started the application using the default profile, and inside the default profile, every password is a valid password.

That's why I'm trying to give an invalid username by just adding 1 towards the end of the username. If I try to send this request, you'll be able to see I'm getting the response in a JSON format like timestamp, status, error, message, path, and the overall status here also you can see I'm getting the 401 with the message, unauthorized. There is a very good chance in real applications or in real prod applications, we may receive a requirement saying that, instead of this response I want to send some other response.

Maybe I want to send different fields or different values. Apart from customizing the body, you may also have a requirement to send your own response header inside the response. To accommodate these kind of custom requirements, first we need to understand how the exceptions are going to be handled inside the Spring Security framework. Once we understand how the Spring Security is handling the exceptions, later on, we can try to customize this response that we're seeing on the Postman.

In general, the Spring Security framework, it is not going to worry about all kind of business exceptions or all kind of runtime exceptions that are going to happen inside your application core. It is only going to worry and handle security related exceptions. So inside that security framework, there are two types of exceptions that may happen. The very first type of exception is AuthenticationException, which may result into the 401 status. 401 indicates that the person or the client application is not authenticated.

So all the exceptions like BadCredentialsException, UsernameNotFoundException, they all come under the category of AuthenticationException. Just like how we have 401, we also have 403 error inside HTTP status codes. 403 indicates forbidden error. That means the person or the client application is properly authenticated but they don't have enough privileges or roles to access a secured API. So in all these kind of scenarios, we are going to get the 403 error and all the exceptions related to 403, they come under the AccessDeniedException.

Basically Spring Security is going to worry on how to handle only these two type of exceptions. Inside Spring Security we have a filter which is going to monitor these two exceptions. So this filter name is ExceptionTranslationFilter. The responsibility of this filter is first it is going to check what is the type of exception received? If it is related to the AuthenticationException, it is going to invoke the AuthenticationEntryPoint related implementations.

So AuthenticationEntryPoint is an interface inside the Spring Security framework, which is responsible to handle all authentication related exceptions. By default, Spring Security provide lot many AuthenticationEntryPoint implementations. So based upon the scenario on the flow, this ExceptionTranslationFilter, it is going to invoke one of the AuthenticationEntryPoint implementation classes. Similarly, in the scenarios where the exception type is AccessDeniedException, then the responsibility of the ExceptionTranslationFilter is to invoke one of the implementation of AccessDeniedHandler interface.

With this, I'm assuming you got some clarity how to build our own custom logic, our custom response that needs to be sent in the scenario of AuthenticationException, and in the scenario of AccessDeniedException. We just have to override these two interfaces and write our own logic to send our own custom response or to execute our own custom logic. I hope you're clear with the role of ExceptionTranslationFilter. Let's try to quickly validate this filter inside the workspace.

Here, I'm going to look for a filter which is ExceptionTranslationFilter. You can read the class documentation they clearly highlighted, it handles any AccessDeniedException and AuthenticationException thrown within the filter chain. Inside Spring Security there are many filters that are going to be executed during the authentication, authorization flow or while handling the common security scenarios. So in all these kind of scenarios, if the code is going to result into the AuthenticationException or AccessDeniedException, then this is the filter which is responsible to handle the same.

Let's go to the method which is doFilter(). Inside these doFilter() methods, you'll be able to see inside the try block, we don't have much of the business logic. They're just trying to invoke the next filter inside the chain. So these are very happy part scenario where if there is no exception inside the flow, then this filter it is not going to do anything other than invoking the next filter inside the filter chain. But in the scenario where if there is an exception happens, then this catch block is going to be executed.

Inside this catch block, if you can scroll down, there is a method invocation, and this method is handleSpringSecurityException(). So let me open this method which is present inside the same class. Inside this method they're trying to check what is the instance of exception. Is this belong to the AuthenticationException or AccessDeniedException? If it is an authentication related exception, they're trying to invoke the handleAuthenticationException().

Otherwise they're going to invoke the handleAccessDeniedException(). Let me open the handleAuthenticationException(). Inside this method they're trying to invoke one more method, which is sendStartAuthentication(). Inside this method you'll be able to see they are invoking one of the implementation of AuthenticationEntryPoint by invoking its commence() method. We are going to discuss in detail about the AuthenticationEntryPoint. For now, hold your thought around the AuthenticationEntryPoint.

Whereas in the scenario of AccessDeniedException, the filter is going to call this method, which is handleAccessDeniedException(). So inside these also there is a logic. If the user is trying to access the secure pages anonymously, then in such scenarios, it is going to invoke the same method, which is sendStartAuthentication() and inside this sendStartAuthentication(), that's still going to invoke the AuthenticationEntryPoint. The reason why they're doing this is in the scenario where someone is trying to access without any credentials, they're going to become anonymous.

For all anonymous scenarios, we should not consider it as AccessDenied flow. We should still consider it as AuthenticationExceptionFlow because they are never authenticated. That's why even though framework can throw AccessDeniedException in some scenarios, first inside this method, they're trying to check whether the exception arrived during the anonymous flow. If it is arrived during the anonymous flow, they will try to invoke the same AuthenticationEntryPoint business logic.

Whereas if the AccessDeniedException happened in a normal authenticated scenario but not the anonymous scenario, then they're going to invoke one of the accessDeniedHandler implementation by calling the handle() method. So let's try to understand what do we have inside the AuthenticationEntryPoint and the AccessDeniedHandler interfaces. So first I'm going to open the AuthenticationEntryPoint interface. You'll be able to see that there is a note saying that used by ExceptionTranslationFilter to commence an authentication schema.

Inside this interface we only have a single abstract method, which is commence(). If you try to understand what are the implementation classes of this interface, you'll be able to see there are so many implementation classes in the scenario of HttpBasicAuthentication where the authentication is failing. Then this BasicAuthenticationEntryPoint is going to be invoked, and inside the commence() method we have the logic of sending the unauthorized status like 401 along with the message which is unauthorized.

Apart from this 401 status and message, they're also trying to send a default response header, which is WWW - Authenticate with the realm details. That's why we are able to see inside the headers. There is a header with the name WWW - Authenticate with the same details, which is basic realm is equal to realm. We can also confirm if this is the AuthenticationEntryPoint being invoked. So let me keep a breakpoint here and try to send the request with the invalid credentials and you'll be able to see that the breakpoint stopped inside the BasicAuthenticationEntryPoint.

So let me release this breakpoint. In case if we're looking to send our own response headers with our own custom ResponseBody, then we just have to define a new class implementing the AuthenticationEntryPoint. By overriding the commence() method, we can define all of our custom logic. We are going to do this in the coming lectures. For now, let me open the interface, which is AccessDeniedHandler. So inside this interface also there is a single abstract method with the name handle().

Inside this handle() method only everyone has to write the logic on what to happen in the scenario of AccessDeniedException. So if I try to see the implementations for this interface, you'll be able to see there are good amount of handler implementation classes. One of the most important one is AccessDeniedHandlerImpl. So by default, this is the handler class that is going to be invoked, which is going to send the 403 status along with the message.

I can keep a breakpoint here, and to get the 403 error, what I need to do is I need to make sure that I'm passing my authentication perfectly without any issues. So that's why I'm trying to send the proper username and password here. Once the authentication is successful, in my scenario, I'm not going to get any exception. To get the 403, what I'm going to do is I'll try to access an API which does not exist. That's why I tried to append one here.

So with this, what is going to happen is, though technically I'm properly authenticated with my credentials, but Spring Security framework, it is going to throw the AccessDeniedException because there is no API with this name. So let me click on this Send button. You can see the breakpoint stopped inside the AccessDeniedHandlerImpl. So if I try to release this breakpoint, you'll be able to see the response with the status 403 and forbidden, and this is the response body that is being built by the Spring Security framework.

If you want to customize this response body, and if you want to send some custom response headers, then what we have to do, it's very simple, we just have to define a implementation class just like this class, and we need to write our own custom logic inside this handle() method. I hope you are getting a sense of how the 401 and 403 exceptions are being handled inside the Spring Security framework. Please remember this filter name, which is ExceptionTranslationFilter.

This is always responsible to forward the request to either AuthenticationEntryPoint or AccessDeniedHandler based upon the exception type. Let's try to define our own AuthenticationEntryPoint in the next lecture. Thank you, bye.

LECTURE 7.8: Session Fixation Attack protection with Spring Security
----------------------------------------

Lecturer: We're going to talk about two important topics which are Session Fixation and Session Hijacking. I'm going to first explain about what is Session Hijacking because it's very simple. Once we are clear about the Session Hijacking, we can talk about Session Fixation by taking a scenario. Session Hijacking is a type of security attack where the attacker is going to steal the session ID from your browser or from the web network. Many organizations they're going to mention the session ID inside the URL itself.

This is not going to be considered safe. Apart from URL few other organizations, they're also going to create the session ID as a cookie and store inside the browser. Inside these two scenarios, if the hijacker steals the session ID using the same session ID, he should be able to perform some action on behalf of the user. Think like I have used a computer in one of the public place, maybe inside a library I use the computer and logged in into some web application and inside this computer I'm going to have the session ID either in the cookie or if it is present inside the URL, any other person, they should be able to see the session ID details inside the browser history.

And there is also a possibility that the hacker can steal the session ID while your request is traveling through the network. So these are all the typical or possible scenarios where your session ID can be hijacked. To avoid Session Hijacking attack scenarios there are multiple approaches. The very first approach the organizations they're going to use is, to use the history HTTPS protocol. If they use the history HTTPS protocol for the communication, then hacker cannot steal the session ID during the network traffic or while your request is traveling throughout the internet.

And the next approach that typically organizations are going to follow is they're going to limit the session ID timeout for short time, like 10 minutes or 15 minutes like we discussed in the previous sections. In this kind of scenarios, even though the end user is trying to use a public computer, if some other person comes after some time, the session ID might have expired. At the same time, few organizations during the login operation, they have a checkbox for the end user to check if they're using a public computer.

In such scenarios, the organizations are going to be very cautious in creating the cookies inside the browser. Instead of creating the cookies inside the user browser, they may switch to some other option. So if you see here in the scenario of session hijacking, there is no role played by the Spring Security directly. So the organization, they have to take multiple measurements like using the history HTTPS protocol, asking the end user if they're using the public computer and having the session timeout with a very short time.

By using all these approaches, we can avoid the Session Hijacking scenario. In simple words, Session Hijacking is a attack every hacker steals your session ID and use on your behalf. I hope you're clear about these Session Hijacking attack. Now let's try to understand what is the Session Fixation Attack? I have mentioned that definition for your reference. Please pause the video and read this definition. If this definition is not clear, don't worry I'm going to make it clear by explaining the definition in a simple words by taking a scenario.

This is the scenario that I'm talking to explain you about the Session Fixation Attack. Think like there is a website with the name fashionmart.com and this website is being used extensionally by the user Emily who often shops online and she also stores her payment details for quick purchase inside these website. So Emily is a normal and good customer. On the other side we have another user with the name Eva. Eva is a hacker and Eva discovers a vulnerability inside the Fashion Mart website which allows Eva to manipulate the session identifiers like session ID.

So let's try to understand how the manipulation of the sessions is going to happen. Initially the hacker, Eva, is going to log in into the website with her own credentials and in this scenario the website is going to provide a session with the session ID like you can see here, so the session ID is ending with 43, so please make a note of it. Now the hacker Eva, she's going to send an email to Emily pretending to be from the Fashion website itself.

So inside this website she's going to highlight some exciting offers saying that we are offering exclusive discounts to our loyal customers. Click here to access your personalized discount. So inside the link there is a session ID embedded. So this session ID belongs to Eva which got created during her login operation. So now think like Emily believes this story or believes this email and without worrying about the session ID in the link, she directly click on this link related to Fashion Mart.

And since there is no session ID or since there is no cookie inside the browser of Emily related to this session ID, what is going to happen is, the browser is going to ask Emily to log in with her own credentials. So that Emily, what she's going to do, she's going to enter her credentials and with that the application is going to use the same session ID for Emily as well. So right now this session ID is going to be mapped to Emily but originally this session ID provided by Eva.

As a final step, what Eva is going to do is Eva in her own computer she will try to access an authorized page or authorized API by using the same session ID that she has initially. This time, as part of the response to Eva, she's going to get all the Emily's related details because right now this session ID is mapped with all the details related to Emily. With that Eva is going to see all the payment information of Emily and Eva should be able to buy some products with the payment information of Emily.

I hope you are clear about these session fixation just like how match fixation is going to happen inside the cricket matches and football matches. Very similarly here also the fixation is happening around the session ID. Initially the hacker is going to generate a session ID and the hacker is going to provide the session ID to some other normal user and if the normal user use the same session ID to enter into the web application, then all the details of the normal user are going to be associated to the session ID which is originally shared by the hacker.

And with that hacker can happily use the session ID to know the normal user details. This is happening because there is a vulnerability inside these Fashion Mart application. Ideally they should have some checks to avoid the Session Fixation Attack. By default, if an application is using Spring Security as a dependency, Spring Security is going to take care of handling the Session Fixation Attack. So let's try to understand how the Spring Security is going to handle this attack.

By default Spring Security framework takes care of handling the Session Fixation Attack. We don't have to make any configurations until unless we want to change that default behavior. How Spring Security is going to handle the Session Fixation Attack is by following three different strategies. The very first strategy is, change a session ID. In this strategy, what is going to happen is, whenever someone is trying to access an application very first time with some random session ID.

Once the end user is authenticated, Spring Security, it is going to simply change the session ID but it is not going to change the details inside the session, which means a brand newSession is not going to be created. Whatever details associated to that session, they're going to be still there inside the session. But this session is going to get a new ID. Let's assume the hacker initially performed the login operation and the hacker gave the session ID abc to normal person.

When the normal person trying to log in into the application with the changeSessionId strategy, the normal person is going to get the newSessionId like def, but this session it is going to have all the details from the previous session. For example, if the previous session has first name as Eva, the same details are going to be available inside this session as well with a different session ID which is def. With this what is going to happen, the hacker will never know what is the new session ID that got generated on the normal person computer and with that he should not be able to see the extra details that are sailed inside this session.

Maybe payment information is stored after the login is completed. So this extra information will never reach to the hacker because the hacker does not know the new session ID that got created. I hope you're clear on what is going to happen on the changeSessionId approach. So this is the default approach that is being used by the Spring Security and Spring Boot framework as of now. So this approach is introduced as part of the servlet 3.21 update.

Since internally, Spring Boot's they're going to rely on the Servlet container and Servlets to create the sessions. Spring boot ended up using this strategy as the default strategy. Now let's try to understand what are the other strategies available. The next strategy available is new session. In this newSession what is going to happen is, for example, first the hacker logged in and the hacker got a session ID which is abc. The same is sent to the normal person.

And the normal person this time, even though he's trying to log in with the session ID abc but behind the scenes a new brand newSession is going to be created with the session ID like def. So inside these brand newSession, the previous session details that are not going to be copied. For example, inside this session, if there is a variable which is first name as Eva, it is not going to be copied to the brand newSession that is getting created here with the session ID def.

But please note that Spring Security related attributes, they're going to be copied into this brand new scenario. So that is the only caveat that you need to be aware whenever you are using the newSession strategy. And at last we have a migrateSession strategy. In this strategy what is going to happen is a brand new session is, going to be created. Into this brand new session, all the previous existing session attributes that are going to be copied.

So when a brand new session created it is also going to get a new session ID. This used to be a default strategy for the Spring Boot versions, which used to use Servlet 3.0 as an backend Servlet container. But right now since they're using Servlet 3.1 as a backing Servlet container change stationary became that default strategy. I hope you are clear with all these three strategies. Now let's try to understand how to change the default strategy. We know by default Spring Security uses the changeSessionId.

If you have scenario where you need to use either of these session strategies like newSession and migrateSession in such scenarios you just have to make these changes. First you need to invoke the sessionManagement() method, to this sessionManagement() method, you need to parse a Lambda expression and inside these Lambda configurations you should be able to invoke the sessionFixation() method. This sessionFixation() method again accepts configurations in the form of Lambda expression.

To this sessionFixation() method, we need to parse configurations by invoking the methods that are available like newSession, migrateSession like you can see here. I'll show you how to do this in few seconds, but before I try to go to the workspace, let me highlight about the option on how to disable the protection provided by the Spring Security. Instead of newSession() method, you can invoke the non() method to disable the Session Fixation Attack protection that is provided by the Spring Security framework.

But don't try to do this until unless like you have your own strategy to handle the Session Fixation Attack. So if you're confident that you handle the Session Fixation Attack through some other approaches, then obviously you can disable the session fixation attack protection provided by the Spring Security by using these none option. Otherwise don't try to disable this. You can either happily live with the default approach or you can use any of the other two approaches like newSession or migrateSession.

So let's go to the workspace and try to understand how to make these configurations. You can go to the any of the ProjectSecurityConfigurated files and here under the sessionManagement() configurations inside these Lambda expression variable just before the invalidSessionUrl(), you can try to invoke the sessionFixation() method. After the sessionFixation() method, I can mention dot to invoke the invalidSessionUrl(). So to this sessionFixation(), I need to parse the configurations using a Lambda expression.

Let me move these configurations down. Now to this sessionFixation() method, I'll try to parse the configurations using a Lambda expression. So first I need to mention sfc, which means SessionFixationConfig. Using the same variable, I need to invoke the one of the strategies like by default we know changeSessionId is the strategy. If you're looking for the migrateSession, you can invoke the same or if you're looking for the newSession, you can invoke the same or if you're looking to disable it, you just have to invoke the none() method.

You can see it's very simple. We can also go to the class which is SessionManagementConfigurer. So inside these we have methods like CreateDefaultSessionFixationProtection() strategy. With the help of this method only Spring Security framework by default it is going to consider changeSessionIdAuthentication() strategy. In case if you're looking to change the strategy, we have to invoke the corresponding methods like newSession(). There is a method.

So if you go to this method, it is going to help you to have a new strategy, which is newSession(). Similarly, we have a migrateSession() method to change, to migrateSession strategy, and at last we also have none() strategy. I hope this all making sense to you. What I'm going to do is I will try to get rid of all these sessionFixation() related configurations because we know by default the Spring Security framework is going to use the changeSessionId strategy and I'm good with that.

I don't want to clutter my application with so many Spring Security configurations, but I'm trying to share all this information for your future reference. In real projects, if you end up into a scenario where you have to handle the Session Fixation Attack by changing the strategy, you can follow the steps that I have mentioned previously. I hope you're clear. Thank you and I'll catch you in the next lecture, bye.

----------------------------------------

Instructor: Many times inside real applications, we may have requirements to handle the authentication events. For example, on successful authentication, you may want to send an email to an end user saying that you have successfully authenticated, just informing the end user about the login operation. This might be required for the super critical applications, and similarly, in the scenarios of authentication failure also, you may want to send an email or you may want to make an entry inside the database that so and so failure attempts happened.

So, these kind of requirements are very common inside real applications. To handle these kind of requirements, Spring Security is going to publish events whenever an authentication is going to be successful and whenever the authentication is a failure. We have an event with the name AuthenticationSuccessEvent, so this is going to be published by the Spring Security Framework whenever the login operation or the authentication operation is successful.

On the similar lines, Spring Security's also going to publish an AuthenticationFailureEvent in the scenarios when the login operation is failed due to invalid credentials or due to any other reason. So, these events, they are going to be published by a class, DefaultAuthenticationEventPublisher, inside the Spring Security Framework. We as developers, if we want to execute some business logic based upon these events, we don't have to make a lot, many changes.

We just have to build event listeners to listen to these success events and failure events. So, how to do that, it's very simple. We need to first create a bean. Inside this bean, we can define normal methods, like onSuccess(), onFailure(). These method names can be anything, but please make sure these methods are accepting the input, same as the AuthenticationSuccessEvent and the AuthenticationFailureEvent, or AbstractAuthenticationFailureEvent.

Sometimes, failures can happen due to multiple reasons. That's why Framework is going to give you all the failure details. Inside these methods, as of now, I just have some logger statements. For example, whenever the AuthenticationSuccessEvent publishes, I'm going to log this message, which is, "Login successful for the user", and what is the username. So, how to get the username? From the success event, I can invoke the getAuthentication() method, and inside the Authentication object, we know we are going to have the named details of the logged in user, the same I'm trying to use here.

And in the scenarios of failure authentication, I'm trying to log an error() message saying that login failed for the user due to the reason, and to this logger message, I'm trying to upend what is the current authenticated user who is trying to authenticate with the help of these failures.getAuthentication().getName(), and similarly, we will know what is the reason if you try to invoke this method, which is getMessage() with the help of getException() method, but we need to make sure we are mentioning these @EventListener annotation.

So, these annotations are not specific to Spring Security Framework. These are from the Spring Boot Framework. When you mention these annotations, what is going to happen is these methods, they're going to be continuously listening for these events, like AuthenticationEvent and AbstractAuthenticationFailureEvent. I hope you are clear. The Spring Security, always, it is going to shout your result, like whether it is a success or failure with these events.

We as developers, it's our responsibility to listen to them with the help of the EventListener annotation, and inside these EventListener methods, we can write any business logic that we want to execute. To keep things simple, right now, inside these methods, I'm just trying to log the messages, but in real applications, your requirements may be more complex, like sending an email, making an audit entry into the database. The requirement can be anything, but the process is going to be similar to what we have discussed.

Before introducing the Lambda style of configurations, everyone used to configure the Spring Security configurations by just invoking all the methods normally, but these approach is right now deprecated. So don't worry much about them. We came here to understand the integration between the Thymeleaf and Spring Security, but not about the Spring Security itself. So that's why I'm going to scroll on this page. And here there is information about the Spring Security Dialect.

So in all the places where you are trying to use the Thymeleaf related templates, you need to make sure you are importing the Spring Security related Dialect. So if you see here, sec is the dialect here, which indicates security. Using this dialect, if you use authorize, to this authorize, if you try to pass the method, which is isAuthenticated(), it's going to give you a value true or false.

And in the scenarios where the user is authenticated, this is going to return true, and with that, this entire due is going to be displayed, otherwise it is not going to be displayed. Similarly, we can check if a given authenticated user has a role with the name ROLE_ADMIN, ROLE_USER, where to discuss about roles and how to build the logic based upon the roles. LECTURE 7.17: Role of SecurityContext & SecurityContextHolder
----------------------------------------

Instructor: We know inside the Spring Security framework, whenever the authentication is completed, for later use, the framework is going to store the already authenticated details inside the SecurityContext. So this is the hierarchy that you need to remember whenever someone is trying to ask you questions around the SecurityContext. First, what is going to happen is, during the authentication process, an Authentication object is going to be created.

Inside this Authentication object, we are going to have details like Principal, which is nothing but the name or the username of the authenticated user, Credentials, which is nothing but password, and the Authorities of the end user. This Authentication object, it also have a Boolean variable indicating whether the authentication is successful or not. Once the authentication action is completed, the Spring Security framework, it is going to store the authentication details inside the object of SecurityContext.

So SecurityContext is an interface. There is an implementation class for this interface with the name SecurityContextImplementation, we are going to explore the same in few minutes, but this SecurityContext is going to be managed by a class with the name SecurityContextHolder. So this holder class is responsible to manage the details inside the SecurityContext. The holder class exposes various methods to clear the SecurityContext, to add new details to the SecurityContext, to update the SecurityContext details.

So all the CRUD operation related to the SecurityContext along with the other utility methods, we should be able to see inside the SecurityContextHolder class. Spring Security framework is going to leverage this holder class to a great extent whenever it is trying to store or deal with the SecurityContext object. We don't have to implement our own SecurityContext or our own SecurityContextHolder, but as a Spring Security developer, you should know about all these important classes and interfaces.

Let's try to understand more details around the SecurityContext and SecurityContextHolder. Like I was telling before, we have an interface with the name SecurityContext inside the framework, and this interface has methods to retrieve the authentication and to set the authentication details. The SecurityContext object is going to be stored inside the SecurityContextHolder. So whenever you are thinking about the SecurityContextHolder, just think about this locker, so just like how we store valuable information inside a strong locker, very similarly, SecurityContextHolder is like a locker to store the objects of SecurityContext.

Here, if you go deep dive into the SecurityContextHolder, by default SecurityContextHolder, it is going to store the SecurityContext by using a strategy called ThreadLocal. Whenever the SecurityContext details are stored inside a ThreadLocal object, what is going to happen is we don't have to explicitly pass on the SecurityContext object to all the methods that are being invoked as part of the same thread. Anywhere, if you're looking to access the Authentication details or the SecurityContext details, we should be able to easily access them without needing to pass the SecurityContext details to all the methods that are being invoked inside a thread.

I'm going to show you how to access the SecurityContext and Authentication objects in the next lecture. For now, I'm assuming you are clear on how the ThreadLocal is going to work. Otherwise let me try to explain very quickly how the ThreadLocal is going to work. So whenever the client is sending a request to the backend application, for each request, there is going to be a new thread is going to be created. So think like these are all threads like T1, T2, T3, and T4.

Each thread may invoke hundreds of different methods during its execution. Think like this T1 is invoking hundred methods. We can't manually pass the SecurityContext object or Authentication object that is stored inside the SecurityContextHolder manually to all these hundred different methods. Each of the thread, they're going to have their own ThreadLocal. So any objects that are stored inside the ThreadLocal, they're going to be access to all the methods that are going to be invoked as part of the thread journey.

So this is how the ThreadLocal is going to work. I hope you're clear. Apart from ThreadLocal, there are other strategies as well that Spring Security supports. We know by default ThreadLocal is going to be used. So this is that default mode, but the 90% of the applications including the production applications, this MODE_THREADLOCAL should work most of the times. We don't have to change this default behavior. But for some special scenarios, there are other modes are available.

For example, there is a mode with the name MODE_INHERITABLETHREADLOCAL. Let me explain you under which scenarios this INHERITABLETHREADLOCAL is going to be used. Think like there is a client application, and there is a backend application. So this client application can be your browser. If a user is trying to send a request to the backend application, a thread is going to be created, which is T1, and inside the backend logic, somewhere you might have written some asynchronous logic.

We have annotations like @Async inside the Spring framework. Whenever you are using this annotation on top of a method, the logic inside that method is going to be executed using a separate asynchronous thread. In such scenario, what is going to happen? A new thread is going to be created by your backend method which is annotated with the @Async annotation. So these threads, we can call them as asynchronous thread. Let's name this asynchronous thread as T2.

Technically, if you see all these threads, they are being processed inside the same request. In these kind of scenarios, whenever you are trying to create the asynchronous threads inside your business logic, you can use the inheritable mode. Inside this mode, what is going to happen is whenever an asynchronous thread is going to be created by the Spring framework, all the details available inside this T1, they're going to be copied into the T2 thread, which is an asynchronous thread.

This way, the SecurityContext details, they're going to be available to the T2 thread as well. If you're not using this INHERITABLE mode, and if you're using the default THREADLOCAL mode, then in such scenarios, this T2 thread is not going to have any information around the SecurityContext. I hope you're clear under which scenarios you need to use the MODE_INHERITABLETHREADLOCAL. At last, we have MODE_GLOBAL. Whenever we are using this mode, all the threads of the application, they are going to see the same SecurityContext instance or object, which means if your application is having thousands of threads, all these thousand threads, they're going to see the same SecurityContext details.

This mode is strictly not applicable for the web applications, because inside web applications we know different users, they're going to use your application. To show the same user details for all the authenticated users, then it is going to make you to work on the weekend without sleep. With that, you may have question then under which scenarios we need to use is MODE_GLOBAL. Think like you are building a desktop application. So usually desktop applications that are going to be used by a same user inside the same system.

So if you have a scenario where you are building the desktop application, which can be used by only one user at a time, then in such scenarios you can use this MODE_GLOBAL strategy. I hope you are clear. Now let's try to understand how to change the strategy from LOCAL to INHERITTHREADLOCAL, or from LOCAL to GLOBAL based upon your requirements. It's very simple. There are two ways. The very first approach is by using an system property with the property name as spring.security.strategy.

To this property, you can pass the values like INHERITABLETHREADLOCAL and GLOBAL. Otherwise, inside your application, you can create a Bean, which is going to set the strategy by invoking the setStrategyName() method, which is available inside the SecurityContextHolder. So you just have to write a method which is going to return initializeBean(). On top of this, you need to make sure you are mentioning the @Bean annotation. From this method, you just have to execute this lambda expression that I have highlighted inside the slide.

I hope you're clear. I'm not going to make any changes inside my web application regarding these holding strategies. The reason is for our application, the default THREADLOCAL is going to be sufficient. 90% of the scenarios, you don't have to change this default strategy. In case if you end up into the scenarios where you have to change this default strategy, then come to this slide, refer to the information that I have provided, and with this information, you should be able to easily switch the holding strategy.

This is a super complex topic. Inside Spring Security interview, if a person is looking to ask difficult questions, then in such scenarios, the interviewer is going to pick the concepts around the holding strategies. But with the discussion that we have done so far, I'm assuming you are clear. Let me show you the SecurityContext interface which is available inside the Spring Security library. Like you can see here, it has only two methods: getAuthentication() and setAuthentication().

Since this is an interface, obviously Spring Security can't create the objects of this interface directly. Instead it is going to leverage the implementation class with the name SecurityContextImpl. It has a constructor, it has a equals() method, getter() method, hashCode() method, setAuthentication() method, toString() method. Next we can try to explore the SecurityContextHolder. This class is also available inside the Spring Security framework.

You'll be able to see all the details that we have discussed so far. By default, it is going to use the MODE_THREADLOCAL. Similarly, there are other strategies like INHERITABLETHREADLOCAL and GLOBAL mode that we have discussed. If you can scroll down inside this class, you'll be able to see the methods which are going to insulate the strategy. And similarly, there is a method to clear the context, and there is a method to get the context. Maybe what I can do is, I'll try to show you the hierarchy of this class, so that it is going to be clear for you.

So these are all the methods. getContext() to get the context details. setContext() to set the context details. Similarly, setStrategyName() to change the strategy details. The framework behind the scenes, it is going to take help from these holder class to deal with the SecurityContext object. I hope you're clear with all the discussion that we have done around the SecurityContextHolder and SecurityContext. In the next lecture, I'll show you how to access the details inside the holder in any of the methods of your application.

Thank you, and I'll catch you in the next lecture, bye.

Instructor: Inside this lecture, let's try to understand how to load the login user details in your business logic or in your controller classes. So this is my controller, which is marked with rest controller. The same kind of strategy you can follow inside any layer. And the second approach is you can directly mention the authentication object as an method input parameter. With this, what is going to happen is whenever the spring security seeing this object is being mentioned as a method input parameter behind the scenes, it is going to load the authentication object from the SecurityContext and provide the same as an input to the method where you are trying to use.

LECTURE 8.2: Understanding and walkthrough of the Angular code - Part 1
----------------------------------------

Instructor: Inside the previous lecture we set up the Angular UI application. As a next step, I'm going to provide you the high level code walkthrough of this Angular UI application. You have a lot many questions around this application, how this application is going to work, how it is going to invoke the backend APIs. To answer all these questions, I'm going to walk through you all the important code present inside this UI application and with that you'll have enough information on how this application is going to work.

Just like how we have source folder inside the Spring Boot application, very similarly inside any angular UI application, there is an src folder. Inside this src folder, under the assets, we're going to maintain all the static files like css files, JavaScript libraries, images, so all the static files that are required for these application I'm trying to maintain inside these assets folder. The next important folder is app. App means application.

Inside this application folder we have various sub folders. The very first important sub folder I want to highlight here is, components. So these components are very similar to the controllers that we have inside Spring Boot application. If we open this components, you'll be able to see there are multiple folders with the name, like account, balance, cards, cart, contact, dashboard, and so on. Each of these folder represent a single component which is responsible to hand delay a specific piece of logic.

For example, all the account related logic is going to present inside the account component. Similarly, balance related logic is going to be presented inside the balance component, followed by cards, contact, dashboard, header, home, loans, login, logout, notices. Components is a very beautiful concept inside Angular framework. Using these components only, we are going to leverage the UI application in a modular style. Inside each of these folder you'll be having three different important files.

The very first important file is, component file itself. Usually the naming convention is what is a component name. Here it is account. followed by component.ts. Ts indicates TypeScript. All the code inside an angular application we are going to build with the help of TypeScript language. TypeScript is an advanced version of JavaScript. It is going to be very similar to JavaScript but it provides more advanced features compared to the JavaScript.

Here, I want to highlight an important note. Though we are writing the logic with the help of TypeScript, but at the end of the day, all these TypeScript logic is going to be converted into a JavaScript logic during the compilation or during the build process. Why this conversion has to happen from TypeScript to JavaScript? It's very simple. LECTURE 8.12: Introduction to CSRF attack
----------------------------------------

Instructor: Let's try to understand what is a CSRF attack. The full description of CSRF is Cross-Site Request Forgery. So, what is the meaning of forgery? If someone tried to exploit you without your knowledge, we call such kind of activity as forgery. Think like someone got you a checkbook. If they try to forge you a signature and try to withdraw the funds from your bank account, then it is going to be considered as a forgery because some bad person is trying to exploit your money without your knowledge.

The same kind of concept works inside the CSRF attack as well. So inside this CSRF attack, what is going to happen is the hacker, he will try to perform an operation in a web application on behalf of a user without their explicit consent. The end user will never know that hacker is performing CSRF attack on him or her. Inside this attack, the hacker will never steal the username, password of the end user or the JSESSIONID or the cookie of the end user.

Instead, he will trick the end user or he will exploit the end user to carry out an action without their will. I know this definition looks very complex and not simple to understand. Most of the users, they will end up clicking on this banner or on this link because everyone want iPhone at 90% off discount. Let's consider our end user, our innocent user decided to click on this link. And with that, let's see what is going to happen. Inside the step three, like I said, the user tempted and clicked on the malicious link provided by the hacker inside their website, evil.com.

So behind this link, what hacker might have done is he might have built a embedded form which can't be seen by the end user. So, as soon as someone click on that link, this script is going to be executed. So inside his HTML page, he will have some hidden form or he will have a form which can't be seen by the normal end user until unless they open the source code of the page and look for the HTML code, they can't see these form that the hacker is maintaining inside their website.

So inside this form, what is happening? The hacker is trying to make a request to that netflix.com backend server with the path netflix.com change email. And this is a POST method. And to this change email path, the hacker is also trying to send a hidden parameter value, which is email with the value as user@evil.com. So what the hacker is trying to do here? The hacker, he's trying to change the email of your account and the email value that he provided belongs to the hacker.

So, as soon as the end user click on the malicious link, this form is going to be submitted. And since this form is making a request to the netflix.com, what browser will do, my innocent browser will attach the cookie which has value abc123 to this request. And with that, what is going to happen? The Netflix backend, it is going to accept these requests, process the request because it receives a proper cookie value. Here, the problem is that netflix.com backend server is not able to differentiate whether the request is coming from a evil website or whether it is coming from their own website.

This is because even the hacker also is trying to send the request to the netflix.com only. He's not sending to some other domain. He's sending the request to the same domain. Since this form is getting invoked from the same browser but from the different tab, the browser is going to still attach the cookie of the netflix.com to this form while it is making a request to the backend of netflix.com. Here, you may have a question which is won't CORS will help us in this kind of scenario?

Because this form is present inside the evil.com website and from the evil.com website, the request will go to the netflix.com website. So, this might be your assumption. But let me highlight you that regardless whether the CORS is implemented or not, still the CSRF attack is possible in this scenario. The reason is this is an embedded form that is maintained by the hacker inside their website. The advantage with the embedded form sees whenever someone is making a request to an action using an embedded form, the browser will think the request is originated from this domain itself.

It'll never know that the embedded form is present inside another domain, which is evil.com. That's why CORS is not going to be helpful in this scenario. I hope you are clear what is a CSRF attack. LECTURE 8.13: Solution to handle CSRF attacks
----------------------------------------

Instructor: Let's try to understand how to handle the CSRF attack, what is the solution that we need to follow to handle the CSRF attack. As of now, the problem is the backend server of netflix.com or any other backend system, they don't have a mechanism to identify if the given request is coming from their own UI website or from the evil.com website. Because both these approaches, they are attaching the JSESSIONID cookie or login-related cookie as part of the request they are making, and with that, the backend server simply processing the request.

To defeat these CSRF attack, we should make our backend server smart enough to detect the request, whether it is coming from the original website or from the evil.com website. To help our backend server, in this scenario, we need to implement a solution with the help of CSRF token. With the help of this CSRF token, my backend server will be able to differentiate whether the request is coming from the original website or from the eil.com website.

I'll explain you the scenario in few minutes, but before that, let me highlight that the CSRF token is a secure random token value that is used to prevent the CSRF attack. The CSRF token value needs to be unique by user session and should be of large random value to make it difficult to guess for the hackers. So we should not have CSRF token with the value like ABCDEF. These kind of small tokens will not be helpful. Whenever we are generating a CSRF token, it should be at least dual-length character, and it should have some random text value so that it is going to be super tough for the hackers to guess the CSRF token value to perform the CSRF attack.

So let's try to replay the same Netflix scenario one more time, but this time we'll try to include the CSRF token solution as part of the scenario. In the very first step, we know, on a Friday night, one of the end user of the netflix.com, he's trying to watch a movie. The end user entered his credentials on the UI of the netflix.com; with that, the netflix.com, it is going to validate the credentials. And this time, along with the cookie related to the authentication or login operation, this time, the backend server, it is also going to generate one more extra value, which is CSRF token value.

A few people, they also call this token as XSRF token value. So this token will have some randomly generated value, so only the backend server will know at this point of time what is this value. Since this token has to be sent back to the UI application, what backend server it's going to do is, it is going to attach this token value as a cookie to the UI application. So just like how it is trying to attach the JSESSIONID cookie or the login-related cookie, similarly, it is also going to attach the XSRF token value as a cookie to the UI application.

I know you may have too many questions at this point of time; please hold your thought. I am going to explain in very few minutes. So now my UI application received two tokens. The very first one, think like it is JSESSIONID, which is going to help to avoid the authentication again and again. And the next cookie is CSRF token itself. So this is what happened in the step 1. Now, in the step 2, the same Netflix user is going to open the evil.com website in another tab of the user.

And inside the evil.com website, he's going to see a malicious link, which is climbing 90% off on the iPhone. Let's imagine our end user tempted and clicked on that malicious link, which make a request to the netflix.com to change the email by using an embedded form. So when this embedded form making a request to the netflix.com backend, the browser is also going to attach the two cookies that got generated. The very first one is login-related cookie and the second one is CSRF cookie.

This time, even though the browser is attaching both the cookies from the evil.com website, but still my backend server, it is going to throw the 403 error. And with that, the CSRF attack is going to be stopped. The hacker is going to get surprised. We'll be throwing an error, boom, 403. Now, you may have a million dollar question here which is how my backend server is differentiating even though the hacker request has two cookies attached. So this can be your question.

So let's try to understand these in detail. So we have two cookies. The very first one is JSESSIONID and the second one is CSRF cookie. So whenever a CSRF solution is implemented by a backend application, we know it is going to generate the CSRF token value during the very first initial GET() operation. It can be a public GET() operation like loading the homepage, or it can be during the login operation. So if your login operation uses GET(), then behind the scenes, these GET() operations, they can process the request, and as part of the response they can send the CSRF cookie.

But next time when the UI application is trying to make a POST() request or a PUT() request or any other delete request, the backend server, it is going to expect the CSRF token value in two places. The very first place is it has to send as part of the request, so it can be inside the Header or it can be inside the Payload. So based upon the agreement that you have with the backend server, accordingly, the UI application has to send this token value.

And the next place is as part of the cookie. Sending the CSRF token value inside the Cookie is going to take care by the browser. We know the browser is always going to attach the cookies related to your domain automatically, so the hacker will be able to send that token value inside the Cookie by leveraging the automatic attaching of the cookies by the browser. But the hacker will not be able to send the CSRF token value as part of the request.

The reason is very simple. In order to send the cookie value inside the RequestHeader or inside the RequestBody, the client application, at the UI application, they have to manually read the cookie value using a JavaScript. Once the cookie value is read by the JavaScript code, inside the same JavaScript code, they're going to populate the CSRF token value inside the Header or inside a Payload. The same kind of operation the hacker can't perform from the JavaScript code inside the evil.com.

Because whenever a JavaScript is being executed from a given domain, the JavaScript code can read only the cookies related to the same domain. So inside the evil.com, what is going to happen, though hacker can manage to build a client-side code with the help of JavaScript code to read the cookie value inside the browser of the end user, but this JavaScript to code is not going to work, because the browser is going to stop evil.com JavaScript code from reading the cookie belongs to the netflix.com.

So this way the hacker will not be able to send the cookie value inside the RequestHeader or RequestPayload. With that, the backend server will easily identify, okay, this time I got the token only as part of the cookie but not as part of the RequestHeader or as part of the RequestBody. And with that, it is going to simply throw the 403 error, whereas in the proper, genuine scenario of netflix.com, the JavaScript code available inside the netflix.com UI website, it will be able to easily read the Cookie value present inside the browser, because the JavaScript code is being executed from the same domain, which is netflix.com.

So this is the most common approach that is used inside the industry to handle the CSRF attack. I hope you're clear. Let's try to implement all the CSRF-related solutions inside our Spring Boot application so that we can process all type of requests properly inside our web application. Thank you, and I'll catch you in the next lecture, bye.

LECTURE 9.1: Authentication Vs Authorization
----------------------------------------

Instructor: As of now, inside our Spring Boot web application, we are only performing the authentication of the end user. Inside this new section, we are going to focus on authorization as well. But before we try to deep dive on how to implement authorization with the help of Spring Security, first let me try to clarify your doubt, which is what is authentication and what is authorization. I tried to highlight some differences between authentication and authorization inside this slide, but before we try to discuss this slide, first let me try to give an real life example.

Imagine you are traveling from New York to London, so just an imagination. There won't be any expenditure here. So whenever you want to travel to other country, obviously we have to go to the airport. At the airport there'll be an main entrance. So I'll call this as main entrance. At the main entrance when you are trying to enter, there will be a security guy. He will try to stop you and he'll ask certain details about your journey and about your identity proof.

So here most of the users, they will show their passport. Along with the passport, they will also show the ticket as well. The security guy will look into that ticket and passport. He'll make sure that your traveling date is today only and you are the right person by checking the name present inside your passport and inside the ticket. So at this point of time, the authentication is happening. So inside authentication, what is going to happen? Someone is going to validate your identity proof.

For example, if I'm traveling, then I need to prove myself that I'm the right person with the name Madan by showing my passport and the ticket also should have the same name Madan. Once I clear the main entrance security, inside the airport, they will be so many gates like there'll be gate one, gate two, gate three, gate four. Similarly, here I can mark five, six, seven. So what is the purpose of these gates? At the each gate, there'll be a plane ready to departure for various cities.

For example, think like a gate number one, it is going to departure to the Singapore and gate number two, it is going to departure to Delhi. And similarly, gate number three, it'll go to Dubai. And gate number four, it'll go to London. This way, each gate will have a plane ready to departure to your specific destination. So once you enter into the airport, if you try to enter into the gate of Singapore, there will be a security check at this point of time.

They will check your ticket. Since your destination inside the ticket is not Singapore, they are going to stop your entry here. So what is happening here? At this point of time, the authorization is happening. As part of the authorization, someone is going to validate whether you have enough privileges to access and resource. So here the resource is a plane. So at this security point, they're not going to check your authentication or your identity.

They'll simply check whether you have proper ticket or whether you have proper privileges to travel to these specific destination. But if the same user goes to the gate number four, where the plane is going to travel to the London destination, at this point of time, the authorization is going to be successful. The reason is very simple. The person has enough privileges to travel to London. What is the privilege here? The airplane ticket is the privilege here.

So this is the real life example that you can always recall whenever someone is asking you about authentication and authorization. With this knowledge, let's try to understand the technical details of authentication and authorization by going to the slide that we were discussing previously. Both authentication and authorization, they both are related to the security concepts only, but there is a clear difference between them. As part of the authentication, the identity of users are going to be checked for providing the access to the system.

So whenever you want to access a website or a mobile application, first they will check your identity. Are you the right user by asking your email or by asking your mobile number, OTPs, passwords. The applications, they'll try to validate your identity. Are you the right person? Whereas coming to the authorization, as part of the authorization, person's or user's authorities or the privileges, they're going to be validated for accessing the resource.

Let's move on to the next difference. Authentication, which in short form we call it as Auth n is always going to be done before the authorization. So there won't be a scenario where the authorization is going to happen first. Always authentication has to complete, followed by authorization is going to come into picture. Authorization, in short form, we can call it as AuthZ. Coming to the what details needed for authentication and authorization, for authentication, obviously, the systems that are going to ask for the user's login details, whereas for the authorization, the systems, they're going to ask for the user's privileges or authorities or roles.

In the case of authentication failure, it is a standard to throw the 401 HTTP error as part of the response. Whereas in the case of authorization failure scenarios, the standard is to return the 403 error code as part of the HTTP response. If you ask me a real project example, I would say, let's consider the bank applications itself. So as part of the bank applications, they're going to be different users, like there'll be a proper bank customer and there'll be a bank employee.

So inside the web application, there'll be different privileges or different roles for a normal bank customer and for the bank employee. So inside the login page of the bank application, it is always going to ask the same details like what is the username and the password. So we don't differentiate the login mechanism regardless of the type of the user who is trying to access the system. Once the authentication is successful, and once the user is logged in into the bank application, the options or the look and feel of the application is going to change based upon the privileges or the roles or the authorities of the logged in user.

For example, a normal bank customer, he will be able to see the details of his own account. He will be able to transfer the amount from his own account. Whereas if you take a bank employee, like supervisor or manager or cashier, for them, they're going to have different privileges, like they will be able to validate the account details of any person. They'll be able to initiate the transfer of the amount from any account. So they're going to have extra privileges or authorities inside the system.

I hope you're clear with the difference between the authentication and authorization. As of now, we are only performing the authentication inside our Spring Boot web application. We don't have any logic checking the roles or authorities or the privileges of the end user with the help of authorization. So throughout this section, we are going to focus on how to implement authorization with the help of Spring Security framework. As part of authorization, what details we are going to check?

We are going to check authorities or roles or privileges. Different organizations, they call these privileges with different jargons. Few organizations, they're going to call them as privileges. Similarly, few organizations, they're going to call them as roles. And similarly, there are few organizations where they call them as authorities. So these are the different jargons that people use inside the industry while trying to implement the authorization.

Coming to the Spring Security framework, the framework is going to use the jargons like roles and authorities. Using these two concepts, we'll be able to implement the authorization inside the Spring Security framework. There is a difference between them. I'm also going to explain what is the difference between them and when to use these concepts. I hope you are excited for this new section. Thank you and I'll catch you in the next lecture, bye.
