LECTURE 9.6: Authority Vs Role in Spring Security
----------------------------------------

Instructor: So far, we implemented authorization with the help of authorities. Apart from authorities, Spring Security also allow us to enforce authorization with the help of ROLES concept. There is a very minute difference between AUTHORITY and ROLE. So let's try to understand this difference between them. Once we discuss the differences between them, you will get the clarity under which scenarios you need to select either AUTHORITY or ROLE. When now we are using AUTHORITY inside Spring Security framework, it is going to represent that we are trying to enforce authorization with the help of individual privilege or an individual action.

For example, the authorities that we have choose, like VIEWACCOUNT, VIEWCARDS, so they represent a specific action or a specific invocation that an end user can do inside a system. Whereas the roles inside Spring Security, they are going to represent a group of privileges or actions. Let's take an example to understand this better. Think like inside your application, you have various actions, like VIEWACCOUNT, VIEWCARDS. Similarly, there might be other actions, like UpdateAccount, UpdateCard.

Similarly, there are many other update related actions. You may also have delete-related actions, like DELETEACCOUNT, DELETECARD. What we can do is instead of configuring these end number of actions with the help of authorities inside Spring Security configurations, we can group certain actions into your role. Maybe what I can do all view related actions or authorities, I can tag them to your role user. Similarly, update related actions, I can tag to a role, manager, and anything that comes under the delete, I can tag to your ROLE admin.

If needed, under admin, I can also tag the update and View Authorities as well. Similarly, under manager, I can tag, update and review related authorities as well. So the grouping of the authorities into your role is going to be driven by your business requirements. So someone from business team or your product owner or your business analyst, they're going to give you the requirements that so and so actions or so and so buttons can be clicked by so-and-so user only.

So once you receive these business requirements, as a developer, you need to do the brainstorming with the other developers and other teams, and accordingly, you need to create the roles by grouping the privileges and actions. Here, you may have a question, which is, what is the advantage that I'm getting if I group my roles using authorities? It's a great question. Let's try to understand the same. Whenever you are grouping your authorities using ROLE, the Spring Security related configuration that you have to do will be minimal.

Usually, inside real projects, there'll be thousands of actions that an end user perform inside an application. So configuring all these thousands of authorities or actions using Spring Security configurations is going to be a cumbersome and tedious process. So to overcome this challenge, we can group the authorities or the privileges or actions into your ROLE. And with that, the number of configurations that you have to do on the Spring Security side, they're going to be minimum.

One more difference between AUTHORITY and ROLE is whenever you are using AUTHORITY, you are going to restrict the access in a fine-grained manner. So what is the meaning of fine-grained manner? Fine-grained manner means you are going very deep while enforcing the authorization. Whereas whenever we are using ROLE, we are going to restrict the access in a course-grained manner. Course-grained means we are going to restrict the access on a high level with the help of roles information.

I hope you're clear with the difference between AUTHORITY and ROLE. Technically, both authorities and roles, they're going to be represented in a very similar way inside the Spring Security framework. They both are going to follow the same contract, which is granted authority. So to make our life easy and to differentiate between the AUTHORITY and ROLE, what Spring Security team they have done is whenever we are configuring the authorities, we just have to represent the authorities directly inside the Spring Security configurations.

But coming to the roles, whenever we are trying to configure the roles inside the Spring Security configuration, we need to make sure all your roles, they have a common prefix, which is ROLE_. If my intention is to configure the role as admin and user, then I need to make sure that I have the prefix ROLE_ as part of the role name inside my authorities table and inside the Spring Security configurations everywhere. So by default, Spring Security framework, it is going to expect you to have a prefix ROLE_.

We know inside real projects, clients will come with the different expectations. There'll be always a client fellow who says, "I want to change that." So instead of ROLE_, you may want to have ACTION_. There won't be any proper reason why they want to change. But we know inside every project, there'll be a person who want to change their default values just for no reason. To save developers from these kind of requirements that are coming from the client, Spring Security team, they let developers define their own prefix that can be followed through the project.

So how to do this, we just have to create a Bean of type GrantedAuthorityDefaults. You just have to define a method, and inside this method, you can create an object of GrantedAuthorityDetails. To this object, you can try to pass the prefix that you want to use. So here, you can see we have mentioned the prefix as MYPREFIX_. So once this bean is created inside your project, Spring Security framework, it is going to expect this prefix as part of all the role names that you have defined inside the database.

One important note that you need to take care here is you need to expose your method as a static method. The reason is to ensure that Spring publishes these prefix-related configurations before initializing the Spring Security method security related configurations. We also have a concept called method security inside Spring Security. We're going to discuss that method security in the coming sections. So inside the method securities also, we can enforce that role-based authorization.

So just to make sure that method security related configurations are not loading first, we need to make sure that this method is created as static. I hope you're clear with the difference between the AUTHORITY and the ROLE. In the next lecture, let's try to change all our authorization configurations from authorities to role. Thank you, and I'll catch you in the next lecture, bye.

Let me explain very quickly how these Spring Security filters, they're going to work internally.

When a request reaches to an Spring boot web application, which also has Spring Security configurations configured, in these kind of scenarios, the request is going to be intercepted by multiple filters. So inside Spring Security framework, we are going to have multiple filters. It is not like only a single filter is going to handle all the functionality. So whatever filters that are going to be activated by the Spring Security for a given request, they are all going to be executed in a chain manner. So once the filter one execution is completed, it needs to call the next to filter inside the chain, like, so here, F1 is going to call the F2, and the F2 is going to call the F3.

Inside the Spring boot applications, once all the Spring Security related filters are executed, the request will be forwarded to the DispatcherServlet. LECTURE 10.2: How to create and configure our own custom filter
----------------------------------------

Instructor: Right now we understand that inside Spring Security framework we should be able to create our own custom filters and these custom filters we should be able to inject in between the security filter chain. But here you may have a million dollar question, which is "How can I create my own custom filter and how can I inject this custom filter into the security filter chain?" So let's try to understand what are the options that we have here?

When we want to create our own custom filter, there are three important or most commonly used approaches. The very first approaches is you should be implementing an interface with the name, Filter. So type Filter and select these All Places and you should be able to see that there is an interface inside the Tomcat Servlet Container library. So this is present inside the package jakarta.servlet. If you try to look for the list of methods available inside this filter interface, there is a single abstract method and there are some default methods as well.

As a developer, whenever you're looking to create your own custom filter, first you need to implement this interface followed by you need to define all your business logic, inside these doFilter() overrided method. So this method, it is going to accept three input parameters. The very first one is ServletRequest, which is going to represent your Servlet request that is coming from the client application, followed by ServletResponse, which is representing the http response that we are going to send to the client applications.

And the third parameter is FilterChain. Like I said before, all the filters inside the Spring Security are inside any Servlet container environment, meaning they're going to be executed in a chain manner. Once you are done executing your own business logic inside your own custom filter using these FilterChain object, you need to make sure you are invoking the next filter inside the chain. So that's the purpose of this third parameter. Apart from this abstract method, this Filter interface, it also has couple of default method.

The very first one is inIt() method. Inside this inIt() method, by default this inIt() method is going to be empty. Similarly, if you look for, destroy() also is an empty method. destroy() is a method which is going to be invoked by the Servlet Container whenever the Servlet is getting destroyed. So most of the times the Servlets are going to be destroyed during the shutdown process of the web application. So if you have some business logic that needs to be executed during the destroy of the filter, then you can define all such logic by wall writing these default method.

In the similar lines, if you're looking to execute some business logic during the initialization of your filter, you can build such logic inside these init filter, usually inIt() method is going to be invoked only during the startup of your web application. In real projects, most of the times inside the inIt() method developers they're going to write some logic related to the connecting to your database or connecting to your data source so that these connection details they will be able to use inside that doFilter() method.

And like I said before, destroy() method is going to be in work during the shutdown process of the application. The logic usually returned by the developers inside the destroy is to release any connections or to close any connections with the database or with any other data source. So any cleanup activities that you want to do, you can achieve that by writing logic inside that destroy() method. So this is the very first approach that you can follow.

So this Filter interface is not specific to the Spring Boot library or this is not specific to the Spring Security library. This Filter interface is available from initial days of Java. So this is the option one and the second option that you can explore is, GenericFilterBean. So there is an abstract class with the name GenericFilterBean and this abstract class is present inside the Spring library or inside the Spring Boot library. This class is not from the Spring Security library, it is from the Spring Boot or Spring library itself.

By extending this GenericFilterBean, you should be able to define your own custom filter. If you see this abstract class, it is also implementing the filter, which we have discussed previously. And inside this method also you will have a method which is doFilter(). So you need to write all your logic inside these doFilter() method. But here you may have a question which is "What is the difference between the Filter option and the GenericFilterBean option?"

It's very simple. Whenever you have a requirement that you want to read some servlet related init parameters that are defined inside your deployment descriptor like web.xml or if you're looking for an option to read the servlet context details or the environment property details, so in all such scenarios you can leverage these abstract class. If you look for the list of methods available inside this abstract class, there are good amount of methods related to Environment, FilterConfig(), ServletContext(), so anytime if you're looking for an option to read the ServletInitParameter, ServletContextDetails or EnvironmentDetails in all such scenarios, you can happily use these GenericFilterBean.

So the filter option is a plain option where you can strictly write your own business logic. If your business logic is a simple business logic, which does not have any dependency on any other parameters that we have discussed as part of GenericFilterBean, then you can happily go with the Filter approach. Otherwise go with the GenericFilterBean approach. Apart from these two approaches, there is one more approach, which is the recommended approach in certain scenarios.

So this approach we can build with the help of OncePerRequestFilter. This filter is also available inside the Spring libraries itself. And this abstract class which is OncePerRequestFilter, you should be able to see that it is extending the GenericFilterBean. The name of this class will give a clue when you have to use this option. What is the name of the class here? OncePerRequestFilter. So whenever you define a filter by extending this abstract class in such scenarios the Spring framework, it is going to guarantee you that your filter is going to be executed only once at max for each request.

There will be certain scenarios where the same request can be processed to multiple times inside the servlet container environment. In such scenarios, if you're looking for an option to execute your business logic only once, then this is the class that you need to construct to create your custom filter. If you're looking for the scenario details under which the filter can be invoked to more number of times, then I would recommend to read the documentation of this class so they have highlighted under which scenarios the filter may be invoked or processed multiple times and how this class is going to help you to execute your business logic only once.

Inside this class there is a method doFilter() as part of this, doFilter() the framework team, they have written a logic to make sure that your custom filter is going to be executed only once. You'll be able to see there are certain scenarios where they are going to proceed without invoking your filter. If this, if condition matches, they're going to skip your filter execution. And similarly here also there is a scenario where they're going to proceed without invoking this filter.

But in the scenarios where all these checks are failed, then they will come to the else block, where they're going to invoke that doFilter() internal method. So this is the method which you need to override inside your custom filter whenever you are extending the OncePerRequestFilter. So inside this doFilterInternal() method only, you need to write all your business logic. This OncePerRequestFilter it also has other useful methods like shouldNotFilter().

This method you can use in the scenarios whenever you want your filter not to be executed under certain scenarios, maybe you may have a requirement that your filter should not be executed for certain MVC parts or for certain rest API parts. So all such logic you can override inside this method and return true from this method, once your conditions are satisfied. So whenever this method returns true, then your filter is not going to be executed otherwise it is always going to be executed for all type of requests.

I hope now you have some clarity on what are the options that we have to define our own custom filter. So now with all these options we are going to create one custom filter. The next challenge that we may have is, "How to inject our own custom filter into the Spring Security filter chain." So let's try to understand how to do the same. If you go to the ProjectSecurityConfig class, we already configured a filter with a method called addFilterAfter().

When we are discussing about the CSRF, we have created a custom filter with the name CsrfCookieFilter. So this filter is extending OncePerRequestFilter. We need to use one of these methods to configure our own custom filter based upon our business requirements. Based upon the inbuilt filter details that you are trying to provide with the help of second param, accordingly, the Spring Security filter chain is going to be executed to accommodate your own custom filter chain. Let's try to explore what is the other method that we have. The other method that we have is addFilterAt(). This configuration will execute your custom filter at the same portion where the BasicAuthenticationFilter is executed. Apart from addFilterAt(), addFilterBefore() and addFilterAfter(), we also have a method which is addFilter(). If you don't mention this @Order annotation, then obviously you're going to get a runtime exception. So here, I just mentioned the BasicAuthenticationFilter as an example, but like I said before, you should be able to configure any Spring Security filter other than BasicAuthenticationFilter. LECTURE 11.1: Opaque Tokens vs JSON Web Tokens (JWT)
----------------------------------------

Instructor: Welcome to the new section. Inside this section, we're going to talk in detail about the tokens and the role that they play during the authentication and authorization. We're also going to learn how to generate the JWT tokens inside our web applications whenever we are using Spring Security framework. As of now, whenever we try to log into our web application, the Spring Security framework or the backend code, it is giving us two different types of tokens.

The very first one is JSESSIONID token, and the other one is XSRF-TOKEN. So both these tokens, they are going to be stored as cookies inside your browser. Any further requests that you're going to make from your UI application to the backend, these two cookies, they're going to be automatically attached to the request on the backend side. The Spring Security framework is going to validate these tokens. So what is the advantage that we're getting with this token?

With the help of JSESSIONID token, we don't have to send the username and password for every request on the backend server. Also, we don't have to perform the authentication for each and every request. So that's the purpose of JSESSIONID token, whereas with the help of XSRF-TOKEN, the Spring Security framework is trying to protect us from the CSRF attacks. So if you see here, these tokens are very simple tokens. They are just some random String values, but in real applications, you may get requirements to generate the tokens based upon advanced formats like JWT tokens.

That's why inside this section, we're going to put a lot of focus around the JWT tokens and in the same process, I'm also going to teach you how to transmit the token from the back into the UI application without the help of cookies. For critical applications, you may have requirement to not store the token details inside the browser cookies as well. Inside such applications, you need to transmit the token from UI to backend back into UI continuously for each request, so these kind of techniques we're going to apply inside our web application to make it more secure.

Inside the software industry in general, two types of token formats are going to be used by the enterprise applications. The two formats are Opaque Tokens and JSON Web Tokens. In short form, we can call these JSON Web Tokens as JWT Tokens. We can also pronounce these JWT tokens as Jot tokens. From now onwards, I'm going to pronounce JSON Web Tokens either as JWT tokens or Jot tokens. Both these pronunciation refers to the same JSON Web Tokens. So we're going to talk in detail about the JSON Web Tokens in the coming lectures, but before that, let me try to teach you what is the difference between these tokens and when to use a specific token format.

The very first token format that we have here is Opaque Tokens. These tokens are typically random String values with no inherent meaning. So there won't be any meaning to your token, just a random String value, which is maintained by your backend server for a user session. So whenever you want to access a security API, you need to send the same Opaque Token, and behind the scenes, the backend server is going to check if there is any user session associated for a given token.

If yes, it is going to allow you to access the secure API. Whenever an application is using Opaque Tokens format, then there is always going to be a dependency on the backend server to validate the Opaque Tokens for each and every request. Let me take a scenario and explain what I'm trying to convey here. In enterprise applications, always the authentication are security-related logic. They're going to be maintained inside the server called auth server.

We're going to discuss what is auth server and how to build it in the coming sections. So these auth servers we're going to build by following the authentication and authorization framework, which is OAuth2. In the coming sections I'm going to discuss about this. For now, I'm just trying to give you an introduction about this authorization server. The purpose of this auth server is this auth server, it is always responsible for authentication and authorization-related logic.

We're not going to put any business logic inside the auth server, only the security-related logic we're going to mention inside this auth server. So whenever an auth server is involved, definitely the other applications that are going to reach out to the auth server to give them a token so that they can access secure APIs. So think like there is an app one and there is an app two. This app one, it is trying to invoke a secured API, maybe think this API as getRecords, so it is going to give some records in the response, and this is a secured API.

So the A1, before it try to invoke the getRecords API of the A2, the A1 application, what it has to do, it has to go to the auth server and get that token by providing the credentials. So the same token the A1 has to send to the A2 and the A2 will validate with the auth server if this token is valid or not. So if the token provided by the A1 is valid, then only the A2 is going to provide the response. Otherwise, it is not going to give any response.

So if you see here, the A2, it is dependent on the auth server to validate this token. This scenario will occur only when we are using the Opaque Tokens, whereas when we try to use JWT format tokens, this A2, it don't have to depend on the auth software. It can directly self-validate the token without reaching to the auth server, so that's the advantage of JWT token. Apart from this advantage, JWT tokens, they're also going to have user-related information as part of the token.

So whenever we are using the JWT format for our tokens, these A1 and the A2 applications will come to know to whom this token belongs, because inside this token itself, there will be some user details. What are the authorities of the end user? What is the expiration time of the token? So all such details, they're going to be present inside the JWT tokens. So JWT tokens is an advanced topic which we're going to discuss in few minutes, but I'm assuming you got some clarity about the Opaque Token and Jot tokens.

So with this knowledge, let's go to our slide. Here, I have highlighted a point for Opaque Tokens, saying that whenever we are using the Opaque Tokens, it requests a call to the authorization server or a dedicated introspection endpoint to validate and obtain user information. Whereas in the scenario of JWT tokens, they can be validated locally by verifying the token signature using a public key without needing a server call. Apart from validating the token locally, whenever we are using Jot tokens, they're going to have user information and claims information directly within the token.

That's why Jot tokens, in other words, we can call them as self-contained tokens. I know you may still have some confusion about Opaque Tokens and JWT tokens. Don't worry about it. Once we discuss everything about the Jot Tokens, then you are going to get more clarity. For now, please note that Opaque Tokens are some random Strings which does not have any meaning. Since they don't have any meaning, every time we need to rely on the authorization server, our dedicated introspection endpoint to validate the token.

Whereas JWT tokens, they're going to have some user information, expiration time, some token signature, using which we can validate if the token is tampered or not locally itself. With this, you may have question, which is, which one of these token formats is better? There is no single answer for your question. It depends upon your scenario. In some scenarios, using Opaque Tokens make more sense, whereas in other scenarios, Jot Tokens, they're going to make more sense.

But in general, majority of the organizations are using Jot Tokens because they provide a lot of flexibility. Here also I have highlighted that Opaque Tokens are suitable for scenarios where token validation by central is feasible, such as within secure internal network, whereas Jot Tokens are ideal for stateless distributed systems where quick token validation is needed without frequent server calls. So these Jot tokens, they are going to be super helpful in the microservice scenarios because microservices are stateless and distributed in nature.

I hope you got some clarity around the most commonly used token formats, which are Opaque Tokens and Jot Tokens. Thank you, and I'll catch you in the next lecture, bye.

LECTURE 11.2: Advantages of Token based Authentication
----------------------------------------

Instructor: Inside this lecture, let me teach you about the advantages of tokens whenever we use them inside the authentication and the authorization process. We know how the tokens they're going to be generated during the authentication process. I have highlighted the steps here. First, the client is going to send a request to the login page, the username and password. So here the client application, it has to submit the actual username and password of the end user.

So the backend server, so this can be an authorization server or a normal Spring Boot-based web application. What it is going to do is it's going to validate the credentials, and if the credentials are correct, it is going to give you a token as a response. The token can be Opaque Token or a JWT token. As of now, our application is generating opaque token. In the coming lectures, we're going to enhance our application to generate the Jot tokens.

So once the token is generated, the same token has to be sent by the client application to the backend server whenever it want to access a secure API. So if this token is valid, the backend server is going to provide a proper successful response. So that is what happening here inside this process. Now let me try to answer your burning question, which is, what are the advantages that we have whenever we use tokens as part of authentication and authorization?

The very first advantage is, whenever we are using tokens, it is going to provide limited exposure of the user credentials inside the network. What does this mean? The end user is going to share the credentials only once that is during the login operation. For all the remaining requests that the end user is going to make, the credentials are not going to be sent inside the network. Instead, the token is going to travel inside the network. So with this, we have one advantage, which is we are not necessarily exposing the user credentials to the network multiple times. In the scenarios when our an enterprise organization saw a suspicious activity where some hacker stole the tokens, what they can do is they can simply rework or invalidate all the tokens issued by the backend server.

So when they invalidate the token, they are not going to actually invalidate the user credentials. So with this, what is going to happen is the end user is never going to be affected due to the data breach. Even if some hacker get holds of all the tokens, the authorization, they don't have to worry much. They just have to revoke or invalidate all the existing tokens so that the end user, when he's trying to make the request, the login page is going to be displayed where the end user can enter actual credentials.

So these are very first advantage around the Security. The next advantage is around the Expiration. Whenever an backend server is issuing an token, it have a flexibility to issue the token with a specific expiration time. The expiration time can be one hour or it can be one day, or it can be one year. So based upon your business requirements, the backends of work can issue the tokens with a given expiration time. So with this what is going to happen, the tokens automatically, they're going to be expired after a specific time so that even if a hacker get hold of all the tokens, they're going to be useless for him because they might have already expired.

Usually for critical applications, the expiration time will be one hour, or sometimes it'll be even 30 minutes as well. So for such critical applications, even if the end user loses his hard token, the damage won't happen much because the token is anyway is going to expire in few minutes or in few hours. The next advantage is around the Self-contained. This advantage comes into picture, whenever we use Jot tokens. Opaque tokens, we know that they don't have any Self-contained information but coming to the JWT tokens, they have the ability to store the necessary information about the logged in user about their roles and authorities.

So from these Self-contained tokens, the client applications who received the token, they should be able to read the user information. They don't have to rely on the backend server or on the authorization server every time to know the end user details. Instead, they can read the token itself to know the user details. I hope you're clear about the Self-contained advantage. The next advantage is around the Reusability. Let me take a scenario to explain you about this Reusability.

Take the scenario of Google. So Google has lot many products under them, like it has maps, it has Gmail, it has photos, it has YouTube. So there are good amount of products under the same company, which is Google or Alphabet. So for all these applications, there is only going to be a single auth server, which is going to issue the tokens. So when an end user logged in into his Gmail account, inside a browser is going to get a token. So this token is going to receive from the auth server.

Since this token is already present inside his browser as part of a cookie, what is going to happen is if this end user, if you try to access another product of the Google inside the same browser, then the authentication is not going to happen one more time. Instead, the same token will be leveraged by these applications like photos, YouTube, and maps, here the end user only logged in into his account once, and the token that the end user received can be used across applications.

So this is where the advantage of Reusability comes into picture. So this concept, we also call it as SSO, which means Single Sign On. You might have observed these behavior inside your enterprise applications as well. Your organization may have multiple internal applications. Are you going to log in into all these multiple applications multiple times? Off course not you are only going to log in once, and the same access token can be leveraged by all other applications as well.

So this kind of behavior, we call it as single sign-on. The name itself is self-explanatory. You are going to sign on into the application only once. Once the token is received, the same token can be used by other applications as well. I hope you got some clarity around the Reusability advantage. The next advantage is Cross-Platform compatibility. The tokens that are going to be generated during the authentication process, they can be used across various platforms and devices.

The same token that is issued by your backend server can be used inside web application, mobile applications, and IoT devices as well. And the last and the greatest advantage is, Statelessness of the tokens. Whenever we are using tokens, they're going to contain all the information to identify the user, eliminating the need for the session state inside an application. Any user information that is going to be required by an application, since it is already going to be available as part of the Jot tokens, the applications, they don't have to remember the user information.

With the help of sessions, with that, your application is going to be capable of becoming Statelessness. This Statelessness feature is a mandatory for microservices. So inside microservices, since we are going to have multiple microservices inside an organization, they should be built with the Statelessness. With this Statelessness, what is going to happen is if one microservice, even though it has multiple instances like I1, I2, and I3, the request can go to any of these instances because the microservice is Statelessness.

So how the Statelessness is assured? With the help of tokens. So any user information that this microservice instance is looking, it has to read the token and it has to understand the user information. I hope you are clear with all that token advantages. LECTURE 11.3: Deep dive about JWT Tokens
----------------------------------------

Instructor: As of now, our Spring Boot web application, it is generating the tokens using the Opaque token format. We are looking to enhance our web application to generate the tokens using the JWT tokens format. In case if you're using Postman for your testing, you'll be able to see the cookies under the response. So this is my response, and under the cookies tab, I have both the tokens like JSESSIONID and the XSRF token. So let's not worry about the XSRF token.

Let's try to enhance our web application to get rid of this JSESSIONID and instead use the Jot token. But before we try to do that, first we need to understand what is the format of Jot token and how to generate them. We're going to spend some good amount of time understanding about all these concepts. Inside this lecture, let's focus on understanding the format of Jot token. We know what is a full form of Jot. JWT means JSON Web Tokens. The reason why they are called a JSON web token is this token implementation uses the JSON format and designed to use for the web request.

In short form, we can call these tokens as Jot tokens as well. I already explained about this in the previous lecture. Jot tokens are the most common and favorite token type that many system use these days due to their special features and advantages. So when we start implementing these tokens inside our web application, you'll also see the advantages of these tokens. These Jot tokens can be used in the scenario of authorization and authentication.

How this is possible is these tokens allow us to store some user-related information inside the token itself, which will reduce the burden of maintaining such details inside the sessions on the client side or the server side. I'm assuming you are already clear about all these basics. Now, let's try to understand the Jot tokens format. Every Jot token, it is going to have three parts separated by a period. So here I have given a sample Jot token.

Whatever you see highlighted in yellow color, we call it as header part. And after the header, there is a period, which is a separator between the header and payload. After this first period, whatever you see highlighted inside the green color, we call that part or component as payload. After the payload, we are again going to have a period, which is going to act as a separator between components inside the Jot tokens. At last, whatever highlighted in white color we call this component as signature.

So this signature component is optional, but both the header and payloads are mandatory always. I know this is a very high-level discussion around the Jot tokens format. Let's try to deep dive into these components of the Jot token and try to understand what kind of information we are going to store inside them. The very first component that we have is Jot header. So inside the header we usually store the metadata information related to the token.

When I say metadata information, it will have information like what is the type of the token, what is the algorithm that we have used to derive the signature of the token? So all these kind of meta-related information, they're going to be present inside the header. So if you see here this header is a JSON, it has a key alg, which means algorithm, followed by type. So both of them they have values, but inside Jot tokens, we are never going to store the direct values inside the token.

Instead, these values we are going to encode with the help of Base64, and the output we're going to store inside the Jot token. So that's the purpose of header. So header is always going to have the metadata information about the token itself. The next component, which we can call it as body or payload, in this component, we can store details related to the user, their roles, which can be used later for the authentication and authorization. Though there is no such limitation on what we can send and how much we can send inside the payload of the Jot token, but we should always put our best efforts to keep this payload component as light as possible.

So here you'll be able to see this is the sample payload JSON object. Inside this, I'm trying to store lot of user-related information, like subject, name, issued at the time. Similarly, we should be able to store their roles, authorities, their email, phone number details. So whatever needed for our business logic, we should be able to store all such information inside the payload of the Jot token. But don't try to store the password of the end user inside the payload because if you try to store the password of the end user inside the payload body, anyone who has access to your token, they should be able to see the password.

The reason is very simple. All your payload data, they're going to be Base64 encoded, and the encoded value they're going to be stored inside the Jot token. Anyone can see the original text by decoding these encoded data. I hope you're clear with the header and payload components. Let's try to understand the purpose of the last component inside the Jot token, which is signature. In other words, we can call these last part of the token as digital signature.

Like I said before, this digital signature is completely optional. The purpose of this digital signature is, using this signature only, the applications they're going to identify whether the token value is tampered or not. Whenever someone tampered the token body value or the header value or the signature value itself, it can be easily detected with the help of this digital signature. I'll try to explain this digital signature in detail in few seconds, but before that, let's try to understand under which scenarios this digital signature is optional.

If you are trying to generate a token for an application which is internal to your organization, and if you're sure that the token is not going to be tampered by the client applications or by your trusted users, in such scenarios, there is no need of digital signature because you have that confidence that no one is going to tamper the tokens inside your own network. But in the scenarios where you are going to generate the tokens for the client applications or for the end users who are going to use your application from the open web, then in such scenarios, you need to make sure that the Jot token also has digital signature.

So first let's try to understand how the digital signature is going to be generated. Later on, I'll try to explain how this digital signature is going to help us from the tampering of the token. In order to generate the digital signature from the token, we need to use one of the hashing algorithm. So this HMACSHA256 is the most commonly-used hashing algorithm. To this hashing algorithm, we need to send the input. So the input is calculated by Base64 URL encoder of the header.

So the header is going to be again encoded with the help of Base64 URL encode format. Later on, we need to add a period, and at last we should also Base64 URL encode the payload. So this string is the very first input to the SHA256 algorithm. And the next input is the secret value that you want to involve. So this secret value, you need to keep carefully with you. You should not lose this secret. If you lose this secret to someone, then they should be able to generate their own tokens, which are going to be accepted by your backend server.

Usually this secret value is going to be maintained carefully on the backend side. Let's try to understand how the tampering is possible and how this tampering is going to be detected with the help of digital signature. Let's imagine one of the end user, he's trying to log in from an UI application. So the end user will enter username and password. As soon as we press Enter, the call will go to the backend application. So this is a backend application.

So inside the backend application, we have the logic to generate the Jot token. If this username and password entered by the end user is valid, my backend server, it is going to generate a Jot token, and it is going to have header, payload, and digital signature. We know how the digital signature is going to be generated by the backend. It is going to use an hashing algorithm. And to this hashing algorithm, it is going to provide the Base64 URL encoding of header payload as first input parameter.

And the second input parameter is a secret which is known to the backend server only. Once the Jot token is generated, this is going to be sent as a response to the browser or to the client application. Let's assume inside the payload or inside the body of the Jot token, the role of the end user is mentioned as user. Let's assume the end user who logged in into the application, he's a hacker, or he's a bad user. So what he's going to do, he will check for the Jot token that he has received inside the response.

He should be able to tamper the token value. So the tampering that he's going to do is he will try to change the role to admin, which means he's trying to elevate his privileges inside the application. So once the role value is changed, he's going to generate the base64 encoded value of the payload, and the same he's going to update inside the Jot token. So this updated Jot token can be sent back to the backend server for the further request. Maybe inside the second request, the end user might try to the admin path with this role admin, and he will be under the assumption that the backend server is going to give you a proper response, but that is not going to happen.

The backend server, which initially generated the token, it is going to validate the token if there is any tampering happen. Since the tampering happened here, it is going to throw an 403 error, and with that, the hacker is going to get a surprise. So let's try to understand how this backend server is going to identify the tampering scenario. To explain you about this tampering scenario, I have this slide. So initially during the login operation, the backend server, it is going to generate this Jot token, which has header, body, payload, and signature.

So inside the signature we are going to have the hashing value. So this hashing value derived by following this formula. So if the end user or if the client application, if they try to tamper even a single character inside the payload or inside the header or inside the signature, it is going to be easily detected by the backend application. How it is going to detect this, whenever it is receiving the Jot token in the future requests, the backend server it is going to perform the same calculation again.

It is going to take the header, payload, and feed as a first input parameter to the same hashing algorithm along with the secret value that is known to the backend server only. If the input of the hashing algorithm is changed by even one character, it is going to get a different hash value as an output. And if the newly-calculated hash value is not matching with the signature value present inside the token itself, then it is going to enter into the not equal scenario.

Otherwise, it is going to enter into the equal scenario. You may have a question here. What if the end user changed the signature itself to match the tampered payload value or tampered header value? So this can be your question. So the hacker can't do that because the hacker don't have the secret value. So if someone get this secret value which is being maintained by the backend, they should be able to generate the successful tokens with whatever data that they want.

So that's why always securing the secret properly inside your backend application is most important. The same I have highlighted here also, the secret is always going to be stored on the backend. So the backend application instead of storing inside the properties files, they may inject the secret value as an environment variable or they can read from a secret vault. So there are many approaches that industry uses. As long as the secret is secured, the token tampering scenario can be easily detected by the backend applications.

I hope you understand this tampering scenario, how it is going to detected by the digital signature part inside the Jot token. Anytime if you want to understand a Jot token value, you can go to your website, which is JWT.io. Inside this website, if you provide the Jot token as an input value, it will display the header value in a plain text followed by payload. At last, it is going to tell you what is the formula that people has used to generate the signature.

Since the hash value can't be decoded to your original value, that's why here they're not able to show the original value like secret and the other input parameters that we have used for hashing. Instead, they simply highlighted the form that is going to be used to generate the signature and to verify the signature. So let's go to this website very quickly and validate one of the Jot token. So this is a website that I was talking previously. Inside this website, they're always going to keep a default Jot token.

In the coming lectures, when we generate our own Jot tokens, we are going to validate them by pasting the Jot token value here. So the algorithm that they're trying to use is HS256. In case if someone is using different hashing algorithm, they need to select the corresponding one, but most of the times HS256 should be good enough.

And this is the payload data representation based upon the encoded value here. And this is the digital signature. How this digital signature is calculated? By using this formula. So the same formula is going to be used during the verification process as well. Think like I'm trying to tamper one of the letter, and you'll be able to see there is an error here. LECTURE 12.1: Introduction to method level security in Spring Security
----------------------------------------

Instructor: As of now, inside our web application, we enforce the security at the API level. But apart from API level security, Spring Security also supports method level security, which means with the help of Spring Security framework, we should be able to enforce security on top of our Java method. Your Java method can be present inside controller layer, service layer, repository layer. The method can be in any layer, but still we should be able to secure our Java methods.

In critical applications, securing the methods is also equally important because at the end of the day, all the Java methods, they're going to hold a business logic. And once the business logic is executed, the Java methods are going to return lot of sensitive data. So whenever you are into these kind of situations where you want to enforce the security on top of your Java methods, you should be able to happily use method level security. So throughout this section, we are going to talk about method level security, how to enable it and how to implement it inside our web application.

To enable the method level security inside any web application, we need to make sure we are mentioning the annotation, which is @EnableMethodSecurity. This annotation you can keep on top of your Spring Boot main class or you can also keep it on top of a configuration class. Method level security is also going to be useful to enforce the authorization rules in the non-web applications. What do I mean by non-web applications? Many times, few organizations, they're going to build a desktop applications.

That means these applications can be used inside a particular desktop and these applications can't be accessed using web APIs or using the browsers. Since these kind of desktop applications are non-web applications, they're not going to have any end points. Enforcing the security with the help of method level security is going to be super helpful so that the business logic or the methods can be invoke by authenticated and authorized users only. When I say method level security, inside Spring Security framework, it supports two different approaches on how we are going to apply the authorization rules on top of a Java method or on top of a business logic.

The very first approach is Invocation authorization. As part of this Invocation authorization, spring security is going to help us to decide whether to invoke a method or not based upon the authorization rules that we are going to define. That's why inside the name of the approach, you can also see invocation. So here, invocation refers to the invoking a method. The next approach is Filtering authorization. We know all our Java methods, they're going to accept lot of input parameters and they also going to return lot of data as part of the response.

With the help of these Filtering authorization approach, we should be able to perform validations and accept the data only if the data satisfies to our filtering criteria or to the authorization criteria that we have mentioned. Similarly, the written type of the method also can be controlled based upon the filtering condition or based upon the authorization condition that we are going to define. I hope you're clear with these two approaches. I'm going to discuss in detail about these two approaches in the coming lectures.

As a next step, let's try to understand more details about the method level security. Like I was mentioning previously, we need to make sure we are mentioning the annotation @EnableMethodSecurity to enable the method level security inside any web application. To this annotation, we should be able to pass three different parameters. The very first one is prePostEnabled, followed by securedEnabled, and jsrf250Enabled. By default, this prePostEnabled is always going to be true whenever you are using these annotation, which is @EnabledMethodSecurity.

When you are mentioning the prePostEnabled as true, which is the default behavior of this annotation. In such scenarios, you should be able to use annotations like @PreAuthorize, @PostAuthorize, @PreFilter, @PostFilter annotations to enforce the authorization rules. So these are the most advanced annotations that are provided by the Spring Security framework. That's why throughout this course, we are also going to use these annotations. Apart from these annotations, we also have some legacy annotations which are @Secured annotation, @RoleAllowed annotation.

If you are looking to use these annotations, you need to make sure you are setting true Boolean value to these parameters during these annotation declaration. Though all these annotations that are going to perform same kind of action, I would recommend you using the @PreAuthorize and @PostAuthorize related annotations because they provide more flexibility and they are more powerful compared to the legacy annotations like @Secured and @RoleAllowed.

I hope you are clear. Let's try to make these changes very quickly inside our Spring Boot web applications so that we can start enforcing the method level security in the coming lectures. Since we are into the new section, I have created a new project with the name springsecsection_12. Inside this project, I need to open the main class, which is EazyBankBackendApplication. On top of this class, I'm going to mention an annotation, which is @EnableMethodSecurity.

We also have another annotation, which is @EnableGlobalMethodSecurity. So this used to be the annotation to activate the method level security in the previous versions of the Spring Security framework. But right now this annotation is completely deprecated and it is no more recommended to use this annotation. But still, you may see this annotation in few of the blocks or old YouTube videos, but I would recommend you award these deprecated annotation and always use EnableMethodSecurity.

In case if you are building an web application based upon the Spring Reactive, then you need to use the EnableReactiveMethodSecurity annotation. Since our Spring Boot web application is based upon the solid style of execution, we need to use EnableMethodSecurity. This annotation it is going to accept lot, many parameters. The very first important parameter that I want to use here is prePostEnabled. So you can see that default behavior is true, that's why I'm not going to mention this parameter, but in case if you're looking to disable the prePostEnabled annotations, which are @PreAuthorize, @PostAuthorize, in such scenarios, you can mention this prePostEnabled as false.

For the other annotations that we have discussed to enable them, we need to set this parameter, which is jsr250Enabled as true and similarly securedEnabled as true. Though, I'm not going to use the annotations of @RoleAllowed and @Secured annotation, but still I'm going to mention these parameters for your reference. So these are the only changes that we have to do to activate the method level security inside of web application. I hope you're clear what is the agenda of this section.

With the method level security, we're going to bring one more layer of security. We know few clients are few business people. They're going to like lot of security. So based upon our business requirements, we should be able to implement method level security as well. So by the end of this section, you're going to master the method level security. LECTURE 12.2: Details about method invocation authorization in method level security
----------------------------------------

Instructor: The very first approach that we can use to implement the method-level security is Invocation authorization. With this approach, we should be able to control whether the method can be invoked or not based upon our authorization rules. So let's try to understand how to implement this Invocation authorization with the help of Spring Security framework. Invocation authorization can be achieved with the help of two important annotations that are available as part of Spring Security framework.

The very first annotation is @PreAuthorize annotation, and the other annotation is @PostAuthorize annotation. So first, let's try to understand what is the purpose of @PreAuthorize annotation. This @PreAuthorize annotation, we should be able to mention these on top of a class or on top of a Java method. The class and Java method, they can be present inside any layer. Regardless of where your Java method and Java class are present, you can happily use this annotation to enforce the authorization rules.

Most of the times, developers, they're going to use this annotation on top of the Java methods. Using them on top of a Java class is very rare scenario. The syntax to use this annotation is first you need to mention @PreAuthorize annotation. To this annotation, we should be able to provide our authorization configurations as an input. Here I have mentioned various flavors. I just mentioned these annotation multiple times on top of my method just to show you the list of common use cases of this annotation.

But in reality, you are not allowed to use this annotation multiple times on top of a method. So to this method, if you pass the hasAuthority, hasRole, hasAnyRole or has any authority methods along with the authority name or role details, behind the scenes, Spring Security framework, it is going to perform the validations, whether a given end user has enough authority or roles to invoke this method. If the end user does not have given role or authorities, then Spring Security, it is going to throw the 403 error.

Here you may have a question, which is, we are already applying the authorization rules on top of our APIs. Then what is the need to apply the same authorization rules on top of a method again? So this can be your question. To answer your question, let's take a real-life example. If you go to any bank, there are multiple layers of security. At the entrance, you're going to have a security guy, and similarly, there'll be security cameras. Similarly, there'll be strong lockers.

So just like how bank is trying to have multiple security layers, similarly, for critical web applications, we will have these kind of requirements to enforce authorization rules at multiple layers. When we enforce the authorization rule on top of a API, the Spring Security, it is only going to perform the authorization checks during the API invocation or MVC path invocation. But as part of that API or MVC path, we may invoke 100 different Java methods.

If the hacker is somehow able to invoke the API without any proper role or proper authority, we should also have some extra check by enforcing these authorization rules with the help of these annotation. So the very first three syntax, I'm assuming you are clear. Now, coming to the fourth syntax where I'm trying to apply the authorization rule, so here you can see my method, which is getLoanDetails(), it is accepting an input parameter with the name username.

So before I try to invoke this method, I can let my Spring Security framework to perform these authorization check. So with this authorization check, what I'm trying to achieve is please invoke this method if the username is equal to the logged in user username; that means only the logged-in user should be able to fetch their own loan records due to these authorization check that I'm trying to enforce. If someone is trying to manage to invoke this method with a different username, they will not be able to invoke it due to the method-level security that we are trying to enforce here.

So this is one style of enforcing the invocation authorization. The other style, like I was telling, it is with the help of @PostAuthorize annotation. This @PostAuthorize annotation, it is going to work exactly opposite of @PreAuthorize annotation. When we enforce an authorization rule with the help of @PreAuthorize annotation, the Java method is never going to be invoked if the authorization check fails; whereas when we're using the @PostAuthorize annotation, the Spring Security framework is not going to perform any authorization checks during the method invocation.

Once the method invocation is completed and the method execution is completed while returning the output from the method, at that point of time, the Spring Security framework, it is going to enforce the authorization checks that we have mentioned here. You may have a question here, which is, under which scenarios we are going to use @PostAuthorize annotation. This seems to be very odd to me why anyone want to invoke a method without authorization but enforce authorization while returning the output.

This can be your question. Let me try to answer your question. Sometimes during the method invocation, you may not have enough information to enforce the authorization. But once the method execution is completed and once the method is trying to return the object, using the return object, you want to enforce authorization. In such scenarios, we can use the @PostAuthorize annotation. There is no meaning to use @PostAuthorize annotation with the hasAuthority, hasRole, and hasAnyRole approaches, because these approaches we can happily use with the @PreAuthorize annotation.

But technically, it is possible to use these styles with the help of @PostAuthorize annotation. But if you try to look at the last syntax or last two configurations that I have, this is the scenario where it is going to make more sense to use @PostAuthorize annotation. So here I'm trying to enforce the authorization based upon the return object that I'm trying to return here. So whatever return object that my method is going to return, it is going to be referred as return object inside my authorization configurations.

Inside this return object, if we have a field with the name username, we can compare it with the logged-in user username. So if the logged-in user username is same as with the username present inside the return object, then only we want to return the object. Otherwise, we want to stop returning that object by throwing the 403 error. Many times we have Java methods where they're not going to accept any input parameter, but they're going to return a good amount of objects.

Think, like, I have a method which is getLoans(). And this method is not going to accept anything, but it is going to return list of loans as an output. Here I can't enforce authorization based upon the username using the @PreAuthorize annotation, because this method, it is not accepting any input parameter; Whereas by inspecting the return object, I will be able to apply the authorization checks with the help of @PostAuthorize annotation. I hope you're clear with these two annotations that we have discussed so far.

Before I try to close this lecture, I want to answer one of your binding question, which is how Spring Security is going to control the method invocations while we are trying to use these annotations. The answer is very simple. Inside Spring, there is a concept of AOP, Aspect Oriented Programming. With the help of this concept, Spring Boot and Spring framework, they should be able to control the method invocations at the runtime. The same concept is being leveraged by the Spring Security framework here to decide whether a method should be invoked or whether a output from a method should be returned or not.

If you don't know the basics of AOP, I would recommend you checking my Spring Boot and Spring course where I discussed about the AOP in detail. Let me show you very quickly what are the classes that are responsible to enforce this method-level security inside the Spring Security framework. You might be curious about it. You need to search for a class, which is AuthorizationManagerBeforeMethodInterceptor. Inside this class, we are going to have all the logic related to the @PreAuthorize annotation, and similarly, there is another class with the name AuthorizationManagerAfterMethodInterceptor.

Inside this class, we are going to have all the logic related to the @PostAuthorize annotation. We also have other classes which are AuthorizationManagerAfterReactive and BeforeReactiveMethodInterceptor. These classes will be leveraged in the scenarios where you are trying to use the Spring React to related annotations. But for now, since we are using the servlet-related annotations, the very first two classes, they're going to play a role. If I open this very first class, inside this class, you have methods like preAuthorize().

So using these methods only, the Spring Security framework is going to enforce the method-level security. In future, whenever you want to debug something during the method-level security, you can put breakpoints inside these methods. We can also quickly validate the other class, which is AuthorizationManagerAfterMethodInterceptor. Inside this class, you'll be able to see the methods related to the postAuthorize() annotation. I hope you understand how to implement invocation authorization inside any web application.

From the next lecture, let's try to see the demo of these @PreAuthorize and @PostAuthorize annotations. Thank you, and I'll catch you in the next lecture, bye.

LECTURE 12.4: Details about filtering authorization in method level security
----------------------------------------

Instructor: We are clear about what is invocation authorization and how to implement it with the help of reauthorize and @PostAuthorized annotation. As a next step, let's try to understand what is Filtering authorization. With the help of this Filtering authorization, we should be able to control what kind of input that a method can accept and what kind of output that a method can return to the client application. Let's try to understand what annotations are involved when we are trying to implement Filtering authorization inside our web applications.

The very first annotation that we can use ease @PreFilter annotation using these @PreFilter annotation, we should be able to control what kind of input that my method can accept, whenever we are looking to use @PreFilter annotation on top of a Java method, we need to make sure that the method is accepting a collection object as an input. So here I have a method which is sale contact inquiry details. So this method is going to accept list of contact objects unless my method is not accepting a list or a collection object, I cannot enforce the Filtering authorization.

That's why as a very first check, please make sure that your method is accepting a collection object as an input parameter. So inside this collection object, we are going to store the contact related objects. So whatever expression that I'm going to write, with the help of @PreFilter annotation, it's going to be applied for each object that I have inside this list input that I have received. Every object that we are going to receive as part of the collection object, we're going to refer it with a standard name, which is filterObject.

So here the filterObject is going to be of data type Contact because we're trying to accept list of Contact as an input. So inside this Contact to Pojo class, there might be a field name with the name, contactName. That's what I'm trying to use here. So if this contactName is not equal to test, then only I want to accept that Contact object as an input inside my List object. Otherwise, if someone is trying to send a contact details with a contactName as test, I'm going to simply ignore such records and I'm not going to send such record as an input to this method.

So this is one style of Filtering authorization. If you want, instead of this test, you can write the logic to check the current authenticated username. I hope you're clear in the similar lines, we also have @PostFilter annotation. The purpose of this @PostFilter annotation is whatever data that you are going to return from your method, it is going to be examined based upon the configurations that you have provided, and accordingly, the data is going to be filtered.

Here I have just changed the annotation from @PreFiltered to @PostFilter, but I'm using the same expression inside the configurations. With this, what is going to happen is inside these list of contact response that I'm going to get from this method, if there is a Contact object with a contactName as test, then search record will never be received by my client application. If required, we can also use @PreFilter and @PostFilter annotations, both of them on a single Java method.

The same applies for @PreAuthorized and @PostAuthorize as well. If you have a business requirement, we can club both @PreAuthorized and @PostAuthorize on top of a single method. But the same annotation is not allowed to use multiple times on top of a Java method. Let's try to validate where inside the spring security framework these @PreFilter and @PostFilter related checks are going to happen.
